LayerFS

Ephemeral Workspaces. Durable Shared History.

LayerFS is the substrate under your agents. Each one mounts a complete, writable Workspace over shared committed history, does its work, commits what it changed, and goes away.

Get started · Website · Docs · Benchmarks · Video · LayerFS × DSH · Community

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/70c25887-86a1-4d81-bd78-571cf1c09a18 > **Status:** [LayerFS 1.1.0](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/releases/tag/v1.1.0), > released as source: the JavaScript API split into `@layerfs/agent`, `@layerfs/backend` > and `@layerfs/runtime` under [`api/`](api/README.md), plus the `layerfs` command. It breaks > code written for 1.0.0; see the [release record](docs/release-notes/1.1.0/README.md). > The results below are 1.0.0's, measured on `main` at `e5c7aaae05`. The Store runs in its Disposable profile only, with no > crash or power-loss durability: use LayerFS for agent work and its history, not > as the only copy of data you cannot rebuild. Since 1.1.0, LayerFS also supports native Windows dsh Live through WSL2 and its own Linux Docker Engine; see the [Windows setup](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/dsh-layerfs#windows-live). ## Try it with LayerFS × DSH

LayerFS runs today through **LayerFS × DSH**, the `dsh-layerfs` plugin for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness). Agents in a dsh session fork Branches, test them in Sandboxes, merge and publish, and the **Work** and **History** tabs show every agent's Branch, live.

## Core ideas

01 · Ephemeral Computing
Compute exists only while a command runs.
02 · Decentralized Agents
Agents on different computers share one serverless Store.
03 · Multiagent Coordination
One project, many Branches. One Branch, many agents.

04 · Recursive Filesystem
Fork recursively any Commit, at any depth.
05 · Ultra Storage Optimization
157 snapshots of a real project in 100 MB, 19.9× smaller than Btrfs + zstd.
06 · Instant Bootstrap
Dependencies come with every mount. No time lost reinstalling.
**And underneath them** | | Supporting idea | In one line | | --- | --- | --- | | | **[07 · Auto Checkpoints](https://layerfs.ai/docs/core-ideas/#idea-checkpoints)** | Every step an agent takes is a checkpoint to return to. | | | **[08 · Append-only Objects](https://layerfs.ai/docs/core-ideas/#idea-immutable)** | Saved objects are never rewritten. The Store only grows. | | | **[09 · Conflict Rules (`.lww`)](https://layerfs.ai/docs/core-ideas/#idea-lww)** | Name the files that should never conflict. The newest edit wins. | | | **[10 · Big File, Small Edit](https://layerfs.ai/docs/core-ideas/#idea-bigfile)** | An edit costs the size of the edit, not the size of the file. | ## See it run

Agents fork Branches, work in Workspaces inside Sandboxes, commit, merge and publish to main. The history grows as they go.

## Results Every suite ran once on `main` at `e5c7aaae05` through the JavaScript SDK. Each row links to its method, environment and receipts. | Suite | What it measures | LayerFS 1.0.0 | | --- | --- | --- | | [fs-bench](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/fs-bench/) | Cloudflare Computer's own twelve-scenario filesystem benchmark, unchanged, same image | **5.20 s vs 8.88 s, 1.71× faster**; faster in 10 of 12 scenarios | | [dsh-dedup](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/dsh-dedup/) | A real project's history, 157 snapshots (4.94 GB of trees), kept as mountable Commits | **100.1 MB vs 1,994.6 MB, 19.9× smaller** than Btrfs + zstd; 156/156 read back | | [pjdfstest](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/pjdfstest/) | POSIX conformance, 8,798 assertions, against kernel overlayfs | **0 unexpected failures**; keeps 76% of overlayfs's passes, every other failure a deliberate format limit | | [fsx](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/fsx/) | Random reads, writes, mapped I/O and truncates, every byte checked | **14/14 pass**, 3.06 M ops, 0 miscompares | | [fsstress](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/fsstress/) | Four concurrent processes, then Commit, remount and compare | **3,755/3,755 entries identical**; 5.21 GB captured by one Commit in 4.9 s | | [smallfile](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/smallfile/) | 100,000 files of 4 KiB, four threads, against libfuse passthrough | **Faster in 9 of 9 operations**, 1.27×–10.71× | | [mdtest](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/mdtest/) | Metadata create, rename and remove, against libfuse passthrough | 0.86–1.28× with 1 process, 1.21–4.22× with 4 | | [fio](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/fio/) | Data I/O bandwidth, against libfuse passthrough | Random read/write mixes 1.49–2.23×; **slower** on sequential write (0.31×), sequential read (0.81×) and random write (0.40×) | One sample per case, seed 1, no best-of. Host: arm64 Mac, Docker Desktop linux/arm64, 8 CPUs, 8.3 GB; host load is recorded per suite. These are release measurements, not a guarantee for your workload. Earlier fs-bench-pro results: [v0.1.4](docs/release-notes/0.1.4/benchmark-closeout.md) · [v0.1.5](docs/release-notes/0.1.5/benchmark-closeout.md) · [v0.1.6](docs/release-notes/0.1.6/benchmark-closeout.md). ## How it works ```text agent tool call ├─ file tool (read, write, edit, grep …) ── SDK, in process ──────► Store └─ Bash ── mount ─► exec ─► commit ─► unmount ▲ └─ Workspace: FUSE view in a Sandbox's daemon ───────────┘ (committed root + its own overlay) ``` - **Store.** One SQLite file holds every Branch, Commit and content object. Each daemon and SDK process opens it directly; there is no database server. - **Branch, Commit, Layer.** A Branch is a writable line of Commits. Publishing a Branch to `main` adds a Layer. Content is chunked and stored once. - **Workspace.** A mount binds the whole committed tree without copying it. Writes go to the Workspace's own overlay until a Commit saves them. Unmount deletes the overlay, never history. - **Conflict.** Two Commits that change the same file are refused with `Conflict`, unless a `.lww` rule says the newest edit wins. ## Prior art LayerFS builds on well-known ideas: layered and union filesystems, copy-on-write snapshots, content-addressed storage and throwaway execution environments. What it adds is putting them together for agents: every tool call gets a full writable tree, and every result becomes a Commit on a Branch in one shared Store. | Prior work | What it shares with LayerFS | Where LayerFS differs | | --- | --- | --- | | **overlayfs, UnionFS, container image layers** | A read-only lower tree with a writable upper layer, which is also where the "layer" name comes from | The upper layer is not just thrown away or kept as a directory: Commit turns it into an immutable snapshot on a Branch, with history, merge and `Conflict`. overlayfs is in the kernel and more complete; LayerFS's FUSE view deliberately omits FIFOs, sockets, device nodes, set-id bits and separate atime/ctime ([pjdfstest](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs-benchmark/blob/main/data/pjdfstest/README.md)) | | **Btrfs and ZFS snapshots, reflinks** | Cheap copy-on-write snapshots that share unchanged data | Sharing is by content, not by extent, so a file that is rewritten in full still stores only its new chunks. On a small-file history of 157 snapshots that gives [19.9× less space than Btrfs + zstd](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs-benchmark/blob/main/data/dsh-dedup/README.md). Btrfs and ZFS also stay cheap for in-place edits of large files, and they are durable, mature kernel filesystems; LayerFS is not ([why Btrfs used more space here](docs/research/layerfs-vs-btrfs-157/REPORT.md#3-why-btrfs-used-more-storage-in-this-workload)) | | **Git worktrees** | One repository, many working copies and branches | A Workspace holds the whole tree, including `.git`, ignored files, dependencies and build output, so a new mount needs no reinstall. Commits happen per tool call, not when someone runs `git commit` | | **[try](https://github.com/binpash/try)** | Run a command against an overlay of your system, then inspect, apply or discard what it changed | `try` works on one machine with one overlay at a time. LayerFS keeps every result as a Commit, and lets many agents branch from any of them and share one Store | | **Apiary and virtual layered file systems** (Potter and Nieh, [USENIX ATC 2010](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenix-atc-10/apiary-easy-use-desktop-application-fault-containment-commodity-operating), [LISA 2011](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/lisa11/tech/full_papers/Potter.pdf)) | Ephemeral containers that start instantly over shared layered filesystems | Apiary isolates desktop applications. LayerFS's target is agent tool calls whose results are kept, branched and merged as history | **Use something else** if you need crash or power-loss durability (the Store runs in its Disposable profile only), full POSIX node types, or top sequential I/O bandwidth ([fio](https://layerfs.ai/benchmarks/fio/)). For a few long-lived [Showing lines 1-300 of 333. Use :301 to continue. Read artifact://0 for full output]

`dsh-layerfs` is a plugin bundle for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (dsh). It changes no dsh code. With the bundle, agents in a dsh session work on a LayerFS project from bash, with the `layerfs` command: one LayerFS SDK call per command (or a short Node script on the SDK for many calls). They fork Branches, test them in Sandboxes, and merge and publish, and you watch every agent's Branch grow, live. The conversation gets **Work** and **History** tabs that draw what each agent did, subagents included. The design is in [#346](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/issues/346). This repository is the LayerFS UI: it moved here from the layerfs repository's `dsh/` folder at `cea713e767` ([#428](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/issues/428)), and builds on a LayerFS checkout named by `LAYERFS_SOURCE` (see [Where LayerFS comes from](#where-layerfs-comes-from)). ## 📦 Install The quickest way is to let a coding agent do it. Paste this into one running on the machine where dsh web will run, in a folder holding clones of this repository and of LayerFS side by side: ```text Set up LayerFS × DSH for me: the dsh-layerfs plugin bundle in DeepSeek Harness (dsh) web, on real LayerFS. 1. Read README.md in https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/dsh-layerfs, the "Install" section and its "Install step by step" steps. It is the guide: follow its steps in order and for this machine's OS (macOS, Linux, or Windows; Windows uses the WSL2 setup below). 2. Check what it needs first: Node 22.19 or newer, pnpm, Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS), network access, a LayerFS checkout (https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs) at the commit in layerfs.json, beside this repository as ../layerfs or named by LAYERFS_SOURCE, and a built deepseek-harness checkout (https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) beside this repository; if there is none, clone it there and run pnpm install && pnpm run build in it. If something is missing that you cannot install, stop and tell me which. 3. Step 1, Install LayerFS: in the LayerFS checkout, build layerfs-daemon and the SDK's native addon in the rust:1.85.1-bookworm image, gather them into the bundle folder, build the runtime image and note its image ID. 4. Step 2: in this repository, run pnpm install and pnpm run build, with LAYERFS_SOURCE set to the LayerFS checkout and DSH_SOURCE to the deepseek-harness checkout (absolute paths). 5. Step 3: make a fresh profile with its own DSH_HOME (not ~/.dsh) and add only dsh-layerfs with dsh's plugin command. Do not add dsh-layerfs-demo. 6. Step 4: write layerfs-host's settings into the profile's cordis.patch.yml: the image ID, plus the bundle folder on macOS or the daemon path on Linux. 7. Step 5: start dsh web with that DSH_HOME and give me the printed http://127.0.0.1:…/?token=… link. 8. Step 6: run pnpm test in this repository, and check that GET /layerfs/status reports no missing settings. Report what you ran and what each step returned. A long cargo build may be run again until it prints Finished, as the guide says; if anything else fails, stop and give me the exact error, and don't retry it on your own. ``` It follows the six steps below and asks before anything it cannot do. Expect a few minutes for the first LayerFS build.
Install step by step: six steps, without an agent These steps take a fresh clone of this repository to LayerFS × DSH in dsh web: first LayerFS itself, then the dsh bundle. Only dsh web is supported. dsh desktop serves the same web client but was not tested. The headless profile composes no preset registry, so it offers no preset; the Host and the bash environment still load there. ### You need | What | For | Notes | |---|---|---| | Node 22.19 or newer, and pnpm | everything | | | A LayerFS checkout at the pinned commit | the SDK, the agent skill, the Linux build | `../layerfs` beside this repository, or `LAYERFS_SOURCE=`; the commit is in [`layerfs.json`](layerfs.json) | | A built deepseek-harness checkout | the client build and dsh itself | `../deepseek-harness` beside this repository, or `DSH_SOURCE=` for the build. In it, `pnpm install && pnpm run build` (its README) | | Docker | Live | Docker Desktop on macOS. It builds LayerFS and runs its Sandboxes | | Network access | step 1 | crates and the base images | Below, `$DSH_LAYERFS` is this repository's absolute path, `$LAYERFS_SOURCE` the LayerFS checkout's and `$DSH` the deepseek-harness checkout's. ### 1. Install LayerFS Live needs three things from the LayerFS checkout: the JavaScript SDK, a Linux build of the daemon and the SDK's native addon, and a runtime image. Nothing is published, so you build them there. **The SDK** is LayerFS #428's three packages in its `api/` folder (`api/agent/sdk`, `api/backend`, `api/runtime`): `@layerfs/agent` (what agents' scripts call), `@layerfs/backend` (background processes, a Workspace's status, storage) and `@layerfs/runtime` (what the Host runs on a LayerFS home: the worker, Init, removal, status). They are plain JavaScript with no dependencies. Run `npm install` once in `$LAYERFS_SOURCE/api` (it only links the three to each other); the Host links them as `link:../../.layerfs/api/agent/sdk`, `…/api/backend` and `…/api/runtime`, and step 2's `pnpm install` first points `.layerfs` at `$LAYERFS_SOURCE`, then makes those links. Only the native addon is built, and a fresh clone has none (`api/binding/layerfs.node`). On macOS and Windows the Host never loads an addon itself: the home's worker runs the Linux build below. On Linux, see step 4. **The `layerfs` command** agents run (`DSH_LAYERFS_CLI`, the Host's wrapper `packages/host/src/agent/cli.js`) runs the checkout's `api/agent/cli/` folder: one `@layerfs/agent` call per command, JSON on stdout ([api/agent/cli/sdk-to-cli.md](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/blob/main/api/agent/cli/sdk-to-cli.md) on the #428 branch). Run `npm --prefix "$LAYERFS_SOURCE/api/agent/cli" install` once: it only links `api/agent/cli/node_modules/@layerfs/agent` to `api/agent/sdk` and downloads nothing. `pnpm install` and `pnpm test` stop with that command when it is missing. **The Linux build.** Build `layerfs-daemon` and the addon in the Rust 1.85.1 image, from the LayerFS checkout's root so Cargo picks up its [`.cargo/config.toml`](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/blob/main/.cargo/config.toml) (the ARM64 profile). This is the recipe of LayerFS's [benchmark/AGENTS.md](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/blob/main/benchmark/AGENTS.md#environment), with the crates fetched into a Docker volume instead of the host's `~/.cargo/registry`: ```sh cd "$LAYERFS_SOURCE" docker pull rust:1.85.1-bookworm docker volume create layerfs-cargo && docker volume create layerfs-target mkdir -p core/target/cluster2-linux docker run --rm -v "$LAYERFS_SOURCE":/work:ro -v layerfs-cargo:/usr/local/cargo/registry -w /work \ rust:1.85.1-bookworm cargo fetch --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml --locked docker run --rm -v "$LAYERFS_SOURCE":/work:ro -v layerfs-target:/work/core/target/cluster2-linux \ -v layerfs-cargo:/usr/local/cargo/registry:ro -e CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/work/core/target/cluster2-linux -w /work \ rust:1.85.1-bookworm cargo build --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml --offline --locked --release -j 6 \ -p layerfs-node --lib -p layerfs-daemon --bins ``` The fetch takes about 30 seconds; on an arm64 Mac with Docker limited to 8 CPUs a cold release build took about 2.5 minutes at `-j 2` and 65 seconds at `-j 6`. Agents keep every command under 2 minutes: put `timeout 110` before `cargo` inside the container (`… rust:1.85.1-bookworm timeout 110 cargo build …`; macOS has no `timeout` command) and run the same command again until it prints `Finished`, since Cargo keeps what it compiled. Then, still in `$LAYERFS_SOURCE`, gather the build into one folder, the `bundle` (any folder Docker Desktop shares, such as one under your home): ```sh BUNDLE=$HOME/layerfs-linux-build mkdir -p "$BUNDLE/api/agent" docker run --rm -v layerfs-target:/t:ro -v "$BUNDLE":/out rust:1.85.1-bookworm sh -c \ "cp /t/release/layerfs-daemon /out/ && cp /t/release/liblayerfs_node.so /out/layerfs.node && chown $(id -u):$(id -g) /out/layerfs-daemon /out/layerfs.node" cp -R api/package.json api/backend api/runtime "$BUNDLE/api/" cp -R api/agent/sdk "$BUNDLE/api/agent/" ``` That folder serves Linux (`daemon` and `LAYERFS_NATIVE`). **macOS and Windows need a sealed bundle**: the home's worker runs the bundle's `api/runtime/src/worker/server.js` and checks every file against its `manifest.json` before it listens, which only the tool below writes. Instead, LayerFS's [`tools/worktree.py`](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/blob/main/tools/worktree.py) ([parallel worktrees](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/blob/main/docs/general/parallel-worktrees.md)), run in `$LAYERFS_SOURCE`, does the same with per-checkout caches, and seals the folder with a `manifest.json`. It needs the runtime image below to exist first, and was not tried for this guide: ```sh python3 tools/worktree.py register --worktree "$LAYERFS_SOURCE" --owner dsh \ --build-image rust:1.85.1-bookworm --runtime-image layerfs-352-runtime:node24 --sandbox-image layerfs-352-runtime:node24 python3 tools/worktree.py prepare --resources --platform linux python3 tools/worktree.py build --resources --platform linux --profile release --jobs 6 ``` `build` prints the sealed folder, `~/.cache/layerfs-worktrees//artifacts/build-linux-`, which serves as `bundle`. **The runtime image** is the Linux image Sandboxes and the macOS worker run. The worker runs `node` from it, so it must carry Node, plus whatever your agents' commands run in Workspaces. The one in use is built from [`tools/runtime/Dockerfile`](tools/runtime/Dockerfile): Node 24.21 on Debian bookworm (the daemon's own base), with corepack's pnpm and yarn prepared offline, and the base's git, python3, gcc and make. ```sh docker build -t layerfs-352-runtime:node24 "$DSH_LAYERFS/tools/runtime" docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' layerfs-352-runtime:node24 # the image setting ``` Use the ID your machine prints: the same build can get a different ID in another image store. Images are never pulled for LayerFS (the worker starts with `--pull never`). ### 2. Build the dsh bundle ```sh cd "$DSH_LAYERFS" LAYERFS_SOURCE="$LAYERFS_SOURCE" pnpm install pnpm run build ``` `pnpm install` first runs [`tools/layerfs-source.mjs`](tools/layerfs-source.mjs), which points the `.layerfs` link at `LAYERFS_SOURCE` (default `../layerfs`) and prints whether that checkout is at the pinned commit; see [Where LayerFS comes from](#where-layerfs-comes-from). `pnpm run build` bundles the client into `packages/client/lib/` with the checkout's `tsdown`: `$DSH_SOURCE/node_modules/.bin/tsdown`, else `../deepseek-harness` beside the repository. Prefer an absolute `DSH_SOURCE` path (`DSH_SOURCE="$DSH" pnpm run build`). Relative paths resolve from `packages/client/`, matching the original build command; an empty value uses the default checkout. The launcher passes the resolved absolute path to the client config. If the checkout or its tsdown CLI is missing, the build stops with `tsdown: No such file or directory`. Run it again after changing the client. ### 3. Make a profile Choose a `DSH_HOME` of your own, so your usual `~/.dsh` is not touched, and use its `web` profile. dsh's `plugin` command makes the profile from the shipped `web` template on first use, installs the packages there with pnpm, and adds each one that is a bundle to the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles`: ```sh export DSH_HOME=$HOME/dsh-layerfs # any empty folder pnpm --dir "$DSH" dsh plugin --profile web add "link:$DSH_LAYERFS/packages/dsh-layerfs" ``` Install `dsh-layerfs` only. The demo bundle `dsh-layerfs-demo` is disabled permanently and is not in this repository. The bundle includes the LayerFS scripted model, switched off; see [Scripted runs](#scripted-runs). The profile is `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/`. Its `package.json` should now read: ```json "dependencies": { "dsh-layerfs": "link:…/dsh-layerfs/packages/dsh-layerfs" }, "dsh": { "profile": { "bundles": ["@deepseek-ai/dsh-base", "@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app", "dsh-layerfs"] } } ``` [Showing lines 1-300 of 738. Rules:

### 1. Install LayerFS

Nothing is published yet, so build a Linux `layerfs-daemon` and the SDK's native addon in the Rust 1.85.1 image, from the repository root. A cold release build takes a few minutes; if it stops, run it again and Cargo keeps what it compiled.

```
cd "$LAYERFS_SOURCE"
docker pull rust:1.85.1-bookworm
docker volume create layerfs-cargo && docker volume create layerfs-target
mkdir -p core/target/cluster2-linux
docker run --rm -v "$LAYERFS_SOURCE":/work:ro -v layerfs-cargo:/usr/local/cargo/registry -w /work \
  rust:1.85.1-bookworm cargo fetch --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml --locked
docker run --rm -v "$LAYERFS_SOURCE":/work:ro -v layerfs-target:/work/core/target/cluster2-linux \
  -v layerfs-cargo:/usr/local/cargo/registry:ro -e CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/work/core/target/cluster2-linux -w /work \
  rust:1.85.1-bookworm cargo build --manifest-path core/Cargo.toml --offline --locked --release -j 6 \
  -p layerfs-node --lib -p layerfs-daemon --bins
```

Gather the build into one folder, the bundle (any folder Docker Desktop shares):

```
BUNDLE=$HOME/layerfs-linux-build
mkdir -p "$BUNDLE/api/agent"
docker run --rm -v layerfs-target:/t:ro -v "$BUNDLE":/out rust:1.85.1-bookworm sh -c \
  "cp /t/release/layerfs-daemon /out/ && cp /t/release/liblayerfs_node.so /out/layerfs.node && chown $(id -u):$(id -g) /out/layerfs-daemon /out/layerfs.node"
cp -R api/package.json api/backend api/runtime "$BUNDLE/api/"
cp -R api/agent/sdk "$BUNDLE/api/agent/"
```

That folder serves Linux. **macOS and Windows need a sealed bundle**: the worker checks every file against the folder's `manifest.json` before it listens, and only LayerFS's `tools/worktree.py build` writes one. The guide has its three commands.

Then build the runtime image that Sandboxes and the macOS worker run, and note its ID:

```
docker build -t layerfs-352-runtime:node24 "$DSH_LAYERFS/tools/runtime"
docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' layerfs-352-runtime:node24     # the image setting
```

Agents' Bash calls use the [`layerfs` command](/docs/sdk/agent/#layerfs), the checkout's`api/agent/cli/` folder. Link it and the packages once; neither command downloads anything:

```
npm --prefix "$LAYERFS_SOURCE/api" install              # links the three packages to each other
npm --prefix "$LAYERFS_SOURCE/api/agent/cli" install    # links the layerfs command to @layerfs/agent
```

### 2. Build the dsh bundle

```
cd "$DSH_LAYERFS"
LAYERFS_SOURCE="$LAYERFS_SOURCE" pnpm install
DSH_SOURCE="$DSH" pnpm run build
```

### 3. Make a profile

Use a `DSH_HOME` of your own, so your usual `~/.dsh` is not touched. dsh's`plugin` command makes the `web` profile and adds the bundle to it:

```
export DSH_HOME=$HOME/dsh-layerfs        # any empty folder
pnpm --dir "$DSH" dsh plugin --profile web add "link:$DSH_LAYERFS/packages/dsh-layerfs"
```

Install `dsh-layerfs` only; the demo bundle is not part of the release.

### 4. Configure Live

dsh writes the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` as `[]`; replace it with the Host's settings. The image is required everywhere, the bundle on macOS and the daemon on Linux:

```
# $DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml
- id: layerfs-host
  config:
    image: "sha256:<64 hex>"                   # the runtime image ID
    bundle: /Users/<you>/layerfs-linux-build    # macOS: the bundle folder
    # daemon: /path/to/layerfs-daemon           # Linux
```

Keep the Host's `home` and `traceDir` in the OS temp area (the default): bash calls in Workspace Write mode may only write there. Until the required settings are in, Init is refused with "LayerFS is not configured", and `GET /layerfs/status` lists what is missing.

### 5. Start dsh web

```
DSH_HOME=$HOME/dsh-layerfs pnpm --dir "$DSH" dsh web --no-open --port 3090
```

Open the printed `http://127.0.0.1:3090/?token=…` link.

### 6. Check

```
cd "$DSH_LAYERFS" && pnpm test
```

It runs the Host, simulator, model, playback and history tests.

## Two real runs

On 2026-10-20, one dsh main agent and seven worker subagents on `deepseek-flash` took an empty LayerFS project to a published, verified `main`, twice: a small app in under an hour and a hard one in an afternoon. Every change went through the SDK as Branches, Commits, merges and publishes.

![Wayfare's History at the end of the run: main at L12 after 147 Commits, with each lane's Branches forking and merging around it](/integrations/runs/wayfare-history.webp)

### Wayfare

A collaborative trip planner in Node 24, with no third-party dependencies.

Time

56 min, 8 agents

History

147 Commits, 31 Branches, 13 Layers

Checks

334/334 tests, A01–A12 pass

Store

1.21 MB on disk for 91.5 MB of snapshots, 27× dedupe

[Full record →](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/dsh-layerfs/tree/main/demo/wayfare)

![Quarry's storage at the end of the run: 8.90 GB on disk for 4.93 TB of history, 913 Commits on 56 Branches](/integrations/runs/quarry-store.webp)

### Quarry

A SQL database in Rust, checked row by row against SQLite, with every build's target/ committed.

Time

4 h 16 min, 8 agents

History

913 Commits, 56 Branches, 9 Layers

Checks

891 tests, 800/800 sqllogictest, Q01–Q12 pass

Store

8.90 GB on disk for 4.93 TB of snapshots, 166× dedupe: less than one copy of main (13.5 GB)

[Full record →](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/dsh-layerfs/tree/main/demo/quarry)

Screenshots from the end of each run, taken with an earlier version of the tab, before it split into Work and History.

## Your first session

### 1. Start a session on a project

In dsh web, start a new session. Its row has the preset chip, which reads **LayerFS × DSH minimalist**, and beside it the **project chip**. Open the project chip and pick **New empty project**, or **Import project…** to choose a folder and import it as a new project; a card under the chip shows the import's progress. The session's project is fixed at its first bash call that uses it.

### 2. Switch to Workspace Write

Set the session's mode to **Workspace Write**. Bash calls then run in dsh's sandbox, which lets LayerFS write its home and traces; subagents inherit the mode.

### 3. Give it a task

The preset already knows the SDK and its rules, so ask for work as you would any agent. Work that splits across subagents shows the most. For example:

![](/agents/cloud.png)A first task Copy prompt

```
Build a small two-page website in this project: a home page and an about page that link to each other, plus a check script (node check.mjs) that fails if either page is missing or a link is broken.

Give each page to its own subagent, each on its own Branch forked from main. Each subagent runs node check.mjs in a Workspace before it commits. When both are done, merge their Branches into one, fix any Conflict, run the check once more, and publish to main.
```

### 4. Watch the Work tab

**Work** sits beside Chat and Trajectory. Its chips are `main` and the Branches. On `main`you see the Store's size and the project terminal, which prints every Branch call (fork, merge, publish) with the agent that made it. A Branch's chip shows its `fs` terminal, the Store reads and writes on that Branch, and one pane per Workspace mounted on it, with the commands run there. Calls appear in step with the run, and **Follow**keeps up with the newest. Click a picture to enlarge it.

![The Work tab on main: storage, 7.51 MB on disk for 2.57 GB of history, the Branches list, and the project terminal with forks, merges and publishes](/integrations/dsh-tutorial-work.webp)

*main: the Store's size and the project terminal.*

![The Work tab on a Branch: the fs terminal with one Commit per apply, and two agents' Workspace panes, one mounted and one unmounted](/integrations/dsh-tutorial-branch.webp)

*A Branch: its fs terminal and each agent's Workspace.*

### 5. Watch History grow

**History** draws every Branch and Commit, which agent made it, and the Layers on `main`, one per publish. It grows as the agents work; **Play** replays it from the start. **File** shows the files at any point and **Storage** what the Store holds.

![The History tab: main with Layers L6 to L10, and agents' Branches forking, committing and merging around it](/integrations/dsh-tutorial-history.webp)

*History: 110 Commits on a dozen Branches, main at L10.*

### 6. Come back to it later

The sidebar's **LayerFS** page has one tab per project: where `main` is and what was published last, History and Files side by side (click a History node to see the files at that point), **New LayerFS session** to start another session on the project, and **Remove project…**, which asks for the project's name first.

## What it adds

### Minimalist preset

"LayerFS × DSH minimalist": bash with background jobs, subagents and compaction, and no read, write or edit tools. Its persona carries an SDK cheat-sheet and the working rules: one Workspace per agent, only the main agent publishes, unmount every Workspace.

### Project chip

Beside the preset chip when you start a session: pick a project, start an empty one, or import a folder as a new project, with the import's progress under the chip.

### Work and History tabs

Beside Chat and Trajectory: the agents' terminals, Branches and Sandboxes, played in step with the run, subagents included; and the project's History, Files and Storage.

### LayerFS page

In the sidebar, one tab per project: History and Files side by side, a new session on the project, and Remove.

Making the profile by hand is the same: that `package.json`, then `pnpm install` in the profile folder. Keep the `pnpm-workspace.yaml` dsh writes there (`nodeLinker: hoisted`), so the bundle shares dsh's own packages. ### 4. Configure Live The Host reads its deployment settings from `layerfs-host` in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` ([`config.js`](packages/host/src/config.js)). dsh writes that file as `[]`; replace the `[]` with the entry list below. | Setting | Linux | macOS | |---|---|---| | `image` | required | required | | `daemon` | required | defaults to `/layerfs-daemon` | | `bundle` | not used | required | | `docker` | `/var/run/docker.sock` by default | the same | | `volumes` | `/var/lib/docker/volumes` by default (Docker's data-root); the Host's user must write it | not used | | `home`, `traceDir` | `/dsh-layerfs/{home,traces}` by default | the same | | `containerPrefix` | `layerfs-` by default: Sandboxes `-` | the same, and the worker `worker` | | `stateDir` | `/dsh-layerfs` by default (bindings, agent names, journals) | the same | An Init without the required settings is refused with "LayerFS is not configured: set … for layerfs-host in the profile patch"; `GET /layerfs/status` lists what is `missing`. ```yaml # $DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml - id: layerfs-host config: image: "sha256:<64 hex>" # step 1's image ID bundle: /Users//layerfs-build # macOS: step 1's sealed bundle (manifest.json) # daemon: /path/to/layerfs-daemon # Linux ``` **On macOS** the Mac runs no Store call itself. `@layerfs/runtime` runs one long-lived Linux container per LayerFS home, the worker (`worker`, `layerfs-worker` by default, labelled `layerfs.role=worker`), and every Store call of the Host and of agents' scripts runs there with the sealed bundle's `layerfs.node`; its endpoint is `/worker/endpoint.json`, and agents get it as `DSH_LAYERFS_WORKER_ENDPOINT`. The Host starts it when it starts; a worker of another build is replaced, so load a new `bundle` only while no dsh run is live. It runs with `--restart unless-stopped`. A call of the Host or an agent that finds it down keeps its own error, and the Host asks the runtime to start it again. **On Linux** the Host and agents' scripts load `@layerfs/agent` in their own process, from `api/agent/sdk` in the LayerFS checkout (through `.layerfs`). It loads the addon from `LAYERFS_NATIVE`, or else `api/binding/layerfs.node`: build it on that machine with `npm --prefix "$LAYERFS_SOURCE/api" run build:native` ([SDK README](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/blob/main/api/README.md#builds-and-compatibility); it needs Cargo 1.85.1 on the host), or set `LAYERFS_NATIVE` in dsh web's environment to a Linux build's `layerfs.node`. `daemon` is that build's `layerfs-daemon`. The Store must be on a local Linux filesystem (ext4, xfs or btrfs). Init installs the Store straight into the new project's volume directory under Docker's volumes directory (`volum… **On Windows** dsh web and the default profile remain on Windows. `@layerfs/runtime` starts one long-lived Node worker in a selected WSL2 distribution, owned by the Host through its stdin. That distribution needs its own running Docker Engine, `/dev/fuse`, Node 22.19 or newer, and a **sealed Linux bundle** from `tools/worktree.py build` (run the build inside WSL, using the private resources described above). Docker Desktop's Windows named pipe is not used by this adapter. Install and build the plugin on Windows with steps 2–3. You can add it to your existing default `web` profile; omit the example's `DSH_HOME` override to do so. Keep that profile's existing patch entries and add: ```yaml - id: layerfs-host config: image: "sha256:" bundle: /home//layerfs-build # sealed Linux bundle, including manifest.json wslDistribution: Ubuntu # wslUser: root # default; must access Docker and its Store volumes # wslNode: /usr/local/bin/node # default; absolute Linux executable path # wslHome: /var/lib/dsh-layerfs-windows/my-profile containerPrefix: layerfs-windows- ``` `daemon` defaults to `/layerfs-daemon`. `bundle`, `daemon`, `wslNode`, and `wslHome` are Linux paths in that distribution. `home`, `traceDir`, and `stateDir` remain Windows paths. The default Linux home is a persistent directory under `/var/lib/dsh-layerfs-windows`, derived from the Windows home. Stores live in the WSL Docker Engine's named volumes on its local Linux filesystem. Never put the Store or Linux discovery home on `/mnt/c` or another Windows-backed mount. The Windows SDK entry preserves the regular SDK API for Host clients and agents. It forwards native calls to the worker; the product SDK and daemon are unchanged. Imports translate drive paths with that distribution's `wslpath`; WSL UNC paths must name the selected distribution. Init reads everything through the Linux filesystem view, including `.git` and ignored files. Windows ACLs are not converted to POSIX metadata; imported metadata is what WSL exposes. The worker validates the sealed bundle's file hashes, listens only on Linux loopback, and requires a random secret delivered over its startup pipe. Its Windows endpoint file is ACL-restricted to the current Windows user and SYSTEM. The Windows SDK source must match the sealed Linux SDK (allowing Git line-ending normalization). Windows binding-file readers share the writers' short admission lock so reads cannot overlap atomic file replacement; failed writes are not retried. Each project's native Store stays open while used and closes after a quiet minute. Project removal explicitly releases its cached Store before deleting the volume. Disposal drains admitted calls without killing mounted commands. Runtime Start and confirmed Restart act on this worker; a silent or busy worker is retained. Changing WSL deployment settings requires restarting dsh. The Host adds its Windows `layerfs.cmd` launcher to dsh's PATH. In a LayerFS-bound session, PowerShell and Command Prompt accept the same CLI commands as macOS, for example `layerfs project list_branches`. The launcher uses the session's `DSH_LAYERFS_CLI` wrapper and preserves stdin and exit codes. Shell syntax still follows the selected shell: PowerShell uses `$env:NAME`, not Bash's `$NAME`, and Bash heredocs are not PowerShell commands. SDK scenarios launch native Node scripts from the Scenarios workspace on Windows. CLI scenarios use a native runner for their limited command notation: quoted arguments, variables, substitutions, literal heredoc input, JSON field selection and tee. Each LayerFS operation invokes the real CLI wrapper; commands inside Linux Workspaces run unchanged. This runner is specific to scripted tests, not a Bash shell for arbitrary agent commands. Linux fixture files check out with LF even when Windows Git uses `core.autocrlf=true`. The dedicated `layerfs-scenarios` preset disables promotion of timed-out foreground commands to background jobs. Windows scripted calls have a 120-second dsh deadline; a 110-second watchdog attempts earlier cancellation. Captured CLI input/output uses temporary files because restricted Windows tokens deny Node named pipes. Explicit background steps keep their normal job ownership. Shipped scenarios use the configured Host image. The runtime Dockerfile includes Rust 1.85.1, SQLite development headers and Chromium/Selenium for Depot, alongside Node and the prepared package managers. Rebuild the image and configure its exact image ID when upgrading from the earlier Node-only image. Every scenario run creates a fresh project and retains earlier projects until explicit cleanup. Adapter or child failures immediately mark the run failed. `pnpm run test:scenarios` checks loading, launchers, fixtures and failure reporting; `node packages/host/tests/windows-cli.mjs` checks the Windows CLI launcher. For later Windows upgrades, keep the Windows checkout and WSL sealed bundle at the same `layerfs.json` pin, rebuild the runtime image when its Dockerfile changes, and run `check:layerfs`, `test:windows` and `test:scenarios` with a 120-second wall limit before live verification. A Cargo download timeout is a network failure: check registry access from the configured Sandbox image. This machine's optional [proxy deployment](docs/windows-live-20261024/deployment/README.md) records its network prerequisites; its addresses are not Windows defaults. WSL, Docker and any configured upstream proxy must be available before starting a run. A request lost before it is sent is `Failed`; a sent request whose reply is lost is `Unknown` and is never replayed. Failed Windows Init attempts retain their volume and Linux discovery state, with the original failure and volume recorded in `windows-init-failures.jsonl` under `stateDir`. Inspect that evidence before deciding how to recover. The macOS container adapter and Windows WSL adapter share the worker codec, but keep separate deployment and lifecycle code. The codec is versioned JSON with explicit binary values, independent of V8 serialization versions. Upgrade the Host and worker together, with no active calls; old V8 workers are incompatible and must be restarted. A protocol failure is reported explicitly and never replays a call. An uncertain Init reply also retains the macOS home and volume, recorded in `init-failures.jsonl` under `stateDir`, so protocol errors cannot trigger deletion of a completed Init. This setup uses the repository pnpm workspace and a dsh source checkout. Packaged dsh desktop and npm/plugin-market installation are not qualified ([#406](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/issues/406)). Docker Desktop volume visibility from a WSL Linux host is a separate unsupported topology; see [#380](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/issues/380). From the dsh checkout, restart your normal Windows `dsh web` server, keeping its usual port (for example `--port 3080`). `GET /layerfs/status` should report an empty `missing` list. The LayerFS runtime page reports both the WSL worker and its Docker Engine. This does not require running a second dsh server in WSL. The [verification record](docs/windows-live-verification-20261022.md) pins the tested source, native bundle, outcomes and platform gaps. **Running two dsh webs on one machine.** The default `home` and `traceDir` are the same for every profile, so two dsh webs would share projects and the worker. Give each its own pair under the OS temp area, and its own `containerPrefix`, since container names are per Docker engine (a worker of another home is refused, never taken over): ```yaml home: /private/var/folders/…/T/dsh-layerfs-/home # node -p "require('fs').realpathSync(require('os').tmpdir())" traceDir: /private/var/folders/…/T/dsh-layerfs-/traces containerPrefix: - ``` Keep both in the OS temp area. Bash calls in Workspace Write mode run in dsh's sandbox, which lets them write only there, and a LayerFS call writes both (a mount elsewhere fails `PermissionDenied`). ### 5. A preset picked in dsh's settings still wins. - The New Session row has a **project chip** beside the preset chip. A Branch's chip shows its `fs` terminal, the Store reads and writes on that Branch, and one pane per Workspace mounted on it, with the commands run there. Calls appear in step with the run, and **Follow** keeps up with the newest.

main: the Store's size and the project terminal.
A Branch: its fs terminal and each agent's Workspace.
**5. Watch History grow.** **History** draws every Branch and Commit, which agent made it, and the Layers on `main`, one per publish. It grows as the agents work; **Play** replays it from the start. **File** shows the files at any point and **Storage** what the Store holds.


History: 110 Commits on a dozen Branches, main at L10.

**6. Come back to it later.** The sidebar's **LayerFS** page shows one project at a time: where `main` is and what was published last, Files beside File, History, Storage and Sandboxes (click a History node to see the files at that point), **New session** to start another session on the project, and, in its ⋯ menu, **Remove project…**, which asks for the project's name first. Its **All projects · Sandboxes** tab is the switcher: the health strip, a card per project that runs a Sandbox, the idle projects, and leftovers.

A project: main's files and its History.
All projects · Sandboxes.
## ✨ What it adds | Piece | Package | Where it shows | |---|---|---| | Host plugin `layerfs-host` | `@dsh-layerfs/host` | bash environment, session records, the `/layerfs` web route | | Client plugin `layerfs-client` | `@dsh-layerfs/client` | Work and History tabs, project chip, LayerFS page (dsh web) | | Agent preset `layerfs-dsh-minimalist` | `dsh-layerfs` (`presets/`) | "LayerFS × DSH minimalist" in the preset menu | | LayerFS scripted model `layerfs-mock` (on by default) | `@dsh-layerfs/mock` | "LayerFS scripted model · …" models, the LayerFS page's Tests tab, the Run bar | | View model | `@dsh-layerfs/model` | used by the client and the Host | | Renderer | `@dsh-layerfs/view` | used by the client | ### Scripted runs The LayerFS scripted model plays scripted agent runs through the real dsh agent loop and tools, without a language model, to test and show the LayerFS UI ([dsh-layerfs#1](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/dsh-layerfs/issues/1)). It ships in the bundle switched on, with this checkout's `scenarios/`; turn `@dsh-layerfs/mock` off on dsh's Plugins page to hide it. Off, nothing of it shows. A run picks its scenario's model on its own Session; dsh would save that pick as the default model for new Sessions, so the plugin keeps scripted models off the default and every other folder keeps your own. - **Scenarios** live in [`scenarios/`](scenarios/), one folder each with a `scenario.json` (loader and full format: [`packages/mock/src/scenario.js`](packages/mock/src/scenario.js)). Every step is one tool call of the minimalist preset (bash, subagent, send_message, the job tools) or a reply, written as an agent would type it. A scenario has one form, its first tag: in a `cli` scenario every bash step is plain `layerfs …` lines; in an `sdk` one every bash step is one inline Node script on the SDK. Half the scenarios are each: `cli` for shop, crew, parallel, checkpoints and conflicts; `sdk` for depot, tour, sandbox, agents and merge. A step that runs commands creates its own Sandbox, mounts one Workspace, runs, commits, unmounts and closes the Sandbox. - **Placeholders.** `{{scenario}}` (the folder's absolute path, written in double quotes) and `{{image}}` (the scenario's runtime image) are filled when it loads. `{{sandbox}}` and `{{commit:}}` are filled when the scripted model sends the step, from what that agent has seen: the last Sandbox number, and the Commit id a step with `commits: []` printed or a received message carried. A Commit id reaches another agent in a `send_message`. - **Checked while it runs.** A bash step's `expect` lists the LayerFS outcome codes its trace lines must show (`workspace.exec:exit:0`, `workspace.commit:Committed|UpToDate`, `workspace.commit:Conflict`), and `exit` its exit status (default 0). Before the agent's next step the scripted model reads the call's trace lines from the Host (its `layerfsTraces` service) and stops the run at the first mismatch. Commands carry no assertions of their own. - **Tags** (`cli`/`sdk`; `node`/`rust` where real builds run; one to three of `conflicts`, `merge`, `publish`, `multi-agent`, `background`, `sandbox`) show as chips on the Tests tab, which filters by them; the loader refuses an unknown tag and also counts each scenario's agents, steps and the LayerFS calls its `expect` checks. - **Replays** (`shop`, `depot`, `crew`) are recorded runs of real agents (layerfs #334, #337, #340) in this format: recorded writes are applied from `changes/` and recorded commands run again in Workspaces. [`tools/replay/convert.mjs`](tools/replay/convert.mjs) generates each folder from the recording at layerfs `0c7d9c47c1^`; rerun it rather than editing by hand, and see each folder's `CONVERSION.md` for what it kept and dropped. Their fixture is the recorded `seed.json` (it holds a `.git/HEAD`, which cannot live here as a file); the plugin writes it out to `/dsh-layerfs-mock/seeds//` when it loads. - **Checking a folder**: `node tools/replay/check.mjs ` loads it and parses every command (`bash -n`, or `node --check` for an SDK script) without running it. - **Checking a finished run**: `node tools/checks/run.mjs ` (the profile is `/profiles/web`) loads the scenario the run played, reads the Host's trace lines for the root and its subagents, and checks the run's state and every `expect`. A recorded `final.json` beside the scenario is reported as not checked: the order and final-tree checks ([`tools/checks/`](tools/checks/)) need a LayerFS client on the project. - **The Tests tab** on the LayerFS page lists every scenario with its latest run. Run all queues every scenario and runs up to 2 at once; each row has Run or Stop. A failed run shows why and keeps its project; Clean up removes the scenario projects no run is using. - **The Run bar** sits above a run's composer: Stop or Run again, and "Step n of m · phase" with a thin bar. - **Each run** gets a new Session in the Scenarios workspace (`/dsh-layerfs-mock/Scenarios`) and its own project, `mock-`, removed and Inited again from the scenario's fixture. A run fails on a failed step (a bash exit other than the step's, or trace lines without its `expect`), a Stop, or after 15 minutes; nothing is retried. The latest run per scenario is kept in `/dsh-layerfs-mock/runs.json`. The Work and History tabs and the LayerFS page are the only LayerFS UI. The standalone HTML pages that used to live in the root `sdk_sim/` (the terminal UI page and its design preview) and their live server are removed; do not build or revive a standalone HTML or TUI page. The simulator (Mocked LayerFS) is removed too. What remains of [`sim/`](sim/) is drawing code: `simulation_engine/model.js` (the views' state shape and `lineDiff`) and `files.js` (the Files tab's helpers), which the client imports, and the avatars (`avatars/`). ## ⚙️ How it works dsh session (agents, subagents, bash) → `layerfs-host` (bash environment, records) → `layerfs` command or LayerFS JS SDK scripts → Store and Sandboxes. A bash call in a session bound to a project gets the project, the SDK and a trace file per agent (`DSH_LAYERFS_*`). Each finished SDK call becomes a `plugin:layerfs/call` record in the calling agent's own session, and the client plugin reads those records back to draw the tabs. On Linux, the Host and the agents' scripts open the Store in their own process. On Windows, Store calls run in the authenticated WSL worker, whose Docker Engine owns the Sandbox volumes. On macOS the Mac runs no Store call itself: `@layerfs/runtime` runs one long-lived Linux container, `layerfs-worker`, and every Store call runs there. An agent creates a Sandbox (`layerfs sandbox create`) and names it in every mount; a Sandbox holds up to 16 Workspaces and closes itself two minutes af… ## 📖 Reference
🔌 Host plugin: bash environment, records, projects, the /layerfs route - **Bash environment.** A bash call in a session bound to a project gets: - `DSH_LAYERFS_PROJECT` and the deployment settings; - `DSH_LAYERFS_SDK` and `DSH_LAYERFS_BACKEND` (file URLs of the Host's wrappers of `@layerfs/agent` and `@layerfs/backend`, `packages/host/src/agent/sdk.js` and `backend.js`), `DSH_LAYERFS_CLI` (the wrapper `agent/cli.js` of the checkout's `api/agent/cli/src/layerfs.js`, which the `layerfs` shim on PATH, `packages/host/src/bin/layerfs`, runs) and `DSH_LAYERFS_SKILL`; - on macOS and Windows, `DSH_LAYERFS_WORKER_ENDPOINT`; - a trace file per agent (`DSH_LAYERFS_TRACE`) and the bash call id as the trace step. LayerFS reads only its own `LAYERFS_*` names, and dsh lets a plugin set only `DSH_*` names in a bash call. Each wrapper therefore loads `packages/host/src/agent/env.js` first, which sets every unset `LAYERFS_` from `DSH_LAYERFS_` in the agent's process, then exposes LayerFS's own entry unchanged (the same exports; the same arguments, output and exit codes for the CLI). A `LAYERFS_` already set is kept. - **Records.** Each finished SDK call becomes a `plugin:layerfs/call` record in the calling agent's own session. The root session gets one `plugin:layerfs/project` record. - **Journal.** Finished lines are also journaled per root session under the state folder, because trace files live in temporary storage. - **Projects.** Each project is attached to at most one workspace folder, or detached; a folder can have several. Init imports a source folder (the workspace folder unless another is chosen) and attaches the new project to the workspace folder. A session uses the folder's only (or last used) project unless it picks another or none. The choice is fixed at the first bash call that uses it. - **Agent names.** Subagents are named by the label their parent gave them. - **Web route.** `/layerfs` sits behind dsh's own connection checks: | Request | Answer | |---|---| | `GET /layerfs/status` | configuration | | `GET /layerfs/workspace?folder=` | a folder's projects | | `POST /layerfs/init {folder, source?, name?, timeout?}` | check the request and start Init; answers its job at once. `timeout`: the Init's limit in ms (a positive whole number; omitted, LayerFS's 300 s); refused `invalid-timeout` (400) otherwise | | `GET /layerfs/init/` | the Init's step (`scan`, `volume`, `import`, `done` or `failed`), the source's file and byte counts, then its project or error | | `GET /layerfs/session/` | project, agents and trace lines of the session's root | | `POST /layerfs/session//project {project}` | choose a project, or `null` for none | | `GET /layerfs/session//state` | the project as `runtime.project.get_state` reports it | | `GET /layerfs/session//tree?ref=` | a Commit's or Layer's files | | `GET /layerfs/projects` | every project and the workspace folder it is attached to | | `GET /layerfs/project//state` | the project as `runtime.project.get_state` reports it, plus who made each node and when Layers and forks happened, from the journals | | `GET /layerfs/project//tree?ref=` | as the session's tree route | | `POST /layerfs/project//attach {folder}` | attach to a workspace folder, or `null` to detach | | `POST /layerfs/project//remove {confirm}` | remove the project; `confirm` must repeat its name | Init is the runtime's (`runtime.project.start_init`): it counts the source (every entry, links not followed, as LayerFS reads it), then makes the volume, then runs LayerFS Init (in the WSL worker on Windows, or a container of its own on macOS), which scans, imports and installs the Store into the volume in one process; it starts no Sandbox. The Host reads the runtime's job every 250 ms (`get_init`: step, counts, and LayerFS's own counts while it imports as `imported`), then binds the project to the folder. The page reads the job every 300 ms and fills the bar from those counts over the Host's totals: scan 0–15%, files 15–95% (bytes plus 4 KB per file), then tree, publish and seal. Removal (`runtime.project.remove`) deletes the project's Sandbox containers, Docker volume and LayerFS home entry, and the Host drops it from the bindings; sessions on it become unbound. It is refused while any container still uses the volume. Workspace files and transcripts stay. A LayerFS project is its home entry, so a removed name can be initialized again at once. The Host reads each project (state and trees) through one shared client (`LayerFS.open`, with `LayerFSBackend` beside it), released after a quiet minute. Reading starts no Sandbox: history comes from the project's Store (in the home's worker on macOS and Windows), and Workspaces only from Sandboxes already running, so a project nobody works on shows its history with no container. The Host keeps each project's last History with its Store version (the eight most recently read): the next read asks the Store whether it changed (`get_history(since)`) and, if not, answers the kept one without listing a Commit; a changed History lists only the Commits it has not seen. The page keeps the History it read too, so the Work and History tabs, and switching between them… The Files pane reads only what is on screen, one SDK call each ([`reads.js`](packages/host/src/reads.js)): a folder a page of up to 1,000 names at a time, a file a window of at most 2,000 lines or 48 KiB. A read costs the same in a small project and a huge one. `node_modules`, `.git` and `.next` start collapsed.
🖥️ Client plugin: Work and History tabs, project chip, LayerFS page - **The Work and History tabs** (beside Chat and Trajectory) replay the root session's lines while one is shown: - Work: the project terminal with agent tags, the Branches and Sandboxes, and the agents' avatars; - History: File, History, Storage and the project's Sandboxes. An unbound session shows Setup: pick one of the folder's projects, or Init. **Playback.** The tab plays calls in step with the run, for real and scripted agents alike ([`playback.ts`](packages/client/src/client/playback.ts)): - each call shows 2 s after it ended, so the gaps on screen are the run's own gaps and the tab never falls behind. The 2 s are longer than the Host poll (1.5 s), so a call is usually here before its time; - calls whose time has passed (the tab opened, a rebuild when an agent is named, a late poll) appear at once, drawn once. Nothing plays twice; - a bash call that mounts, runs, commits and unmounts a Workspace within a second shows each step at its time, and the Workspace's pane then fades out over 1.2 s ("unmounted"), a trail kept by the view only ([`view.js`](packages/view/src/view.js)). **Terminals and their command lines.** Every SDK call an agent makes prints one command line in one terminal. The single table for both is [`packages/model/src/cli.js`](packages/model/src/cli.js); `node packages/model/tests/cli.mjs` fails when an SDK or operator method has no row there. | Terminal | Prints | Calls | | --- | --- | --- | | project (one per project) | the project and its Branches | `project.*`, `branch.*`, and a mount that failed (it has no pane); an older trace's `sandbox.create` and `sandbox.close` | | fs (one per Branch) | Store reads and writes on that Branch | `fs.*` | | workspace (one pane per mounted Workspace) | the Workspace's life and the commands run in it | `workspace.mount`, `workspace.exec`, `workspace.commit`, `workspace.unmount`, the backend's `daemon.workspace.status` and `daemon.process.start` and `.cancel` (an older trace's `sandbox.*` and `operator.process.*` forms too) | | none | the client's own calls and reads | `project.list_sandboxes`, `sandbox.list_workspaces`, the backend's other calls, an older trace's operator reads | A command line is ` [--optional value] [-m "message"]`, using the SDK's own group and method names: `branch merge feature try-ui release -m "join"`, `fs read /app/page.tsx --start-line 5`, `workspace commit -m "add hero" --force`. - Required arguments are positional, in SDK order. Optional ones are `--kebab-case` flags shown only when they differ from the SDK default; a true boolean is a bare flag (`--force`, `--discard`). - An image is shortened to `sha256:` and 12 hex digits. File content is never printed, and `fs apply` shows its change count. - A line does not repeat what its terminal names. The fs terminal hides the `fs` group and the Branch (`read /app/page.tsx`); a workspace pane hides the `workspace` group, the Sandbox and the path (`commit -m "add hero"`, `unmount --discard`), but keeps the operator's `process cancel`. The project terminal prints every group. `fs diff_files` prints both of its refs. - A command run in a Workspace prints as the shell command itself, and a background start ends with ` &`. - Reads (`list_*`, `diff_*`, `fs read/list/stat/grep/glob/blame/diff_files`, `workspace status`) and `workspace mount` are dimmed. - A call with no row prints its own name, dimmed, in the project terminal. The composer is hidden while the tab shows; switch to Chat to send a message. - **The project chip** sits in the New Session row beside the preset chip, drawn like dsh's own chips. Its menu lists the folder's projects and "No LayerFS", with "Import project…" pinned below. Like "Add workspace…", Import opens the directory picker (Finder in dsh web on a Mac); the chosen folder becomes a new project attached to the workspace folder and is chosen for the session. While it imports, a card under the chip shows the percentage, the step with its counts ("Importing 12,000 of 30,000 files · 40 MB of 90 MB") and the elapsed time over a bar. The bar moves without a fraction while the Host counts the source; the Init dialog shows the same. - **The LayerFS page** (sidebar) has one tab per project. Each shows: - ellen_joe, with a line on where `main` is and what was published last; - the workspace the project is attached to, which you can change or detach (a session already on the project keeps it); - History and Files side by side, where clicking a History node shows Files at that point; - "New LayerFS session" in the attached workspace, on the preset; - "Remove project…", which asks for the project's name before removing it. Workspaces without a project offer Init. - **The Init dialog** (Setup and the page) imports the workspace folder by default. "Choose folder…" browses for another source: in the page where dsh offers it, otherwise with the native picker. The project is attached to the workspace folder either way. The name is optional and defaults to the source folder's.
🎛️ Preset The preset has bash with background jobs, subagents (spawn) with their control tools, and compaction. It has no read, write or edit tools. Its persona carries: - an SDK cheat-sheet with a stdin script template; - the working rules: one Workspace per agent, merge conflicts belong to whoever merged, only the main agent publishes, run again on `Busy`, unmount every Workspace. Run the preset's sessions in Workspace Write mode; subagents inherit it.
🧪 Known limits - `demo-workspace` is inside this repository. A turn's "Edited" card lists every change made in the repository during the turn, including other work in the checkout.
## ⚠️ Limits - Only dsh web is checked. dsh desktop serves the same web client but was not tested; the headless profile has no preset registry, so the preset is not offered there. - A session's project is fixed at its first bash call that uses it. - Sessions run in Workspace Write mode. Windows defaults agent traces to `/.dsh-layerfs-traces`, because its restricted shell can write the workspace and its private temp directory, but not the server’s temp directory. The Host retains each trace path across restarts. An explicit `traceDir` must be writable by the agents. Other platforms keep the default traces in the OS temp area. - Everything else follows LayerFS's platform limits: Store calls need Linux and a local ext4, xfs or btrfs filesystem, which on macOS the worker's container provides. - Windows Live uses WSL2 and its Linux Docker Engine through the Windows adapter; native Windows Store execution remains unsupported. Sim's local `/bin/sh` executor is not ported to Windows. macOS execution was not rerun for this change. ## 🧰 Develop | Command | Does | |---|---| | `pnpm test` | Host, scripted model, model, playback and checks tests, with LayerFS stubbed; under 10 seconds | | `pnpm run link:layerfs` | points `.layerfs` at `LAYERFS_SOURCE` (default `../layerfs`) | | `pnpm run check:layerfs` | fails unless `LAYERFS_SOURCE` (default `../layerfs`) is a LayerFS checkout at the commit in `layerfs.json` | | `pnpm run build` | the client bundle, with deepseek-harness's tsdown (`DSH_SOURCE`) | | `node tools/check-session.mjs '' ` | checks that a session's tab draws what LayerFS reports: Branches, heads, `main`, Sandboxes, which agent made each Commit and Layer, and bash-call groups | `assets/` holds unlicensed character art and is never committed. `lib/` is build output. ### Where LayerFS comes from Nothing of LayerFS is published yet, so this repository builds on a LayerFS checkout ([#428 §8](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/blob/main/core/docs/issues/428/README.md#8-versions-and-distribution)): - **`LAYERFS_SOURCE`** names it: a path, relative to this repository's root or absolute. Unset, it is `../layerfs` beside this repository. - **[`layerfs.json`](layerfs.json)** pins it: the default path and the LayerFS commit this repository was moved and tested at. - **`.layerfs`** (git-ignored) is a link to it. `pnpm install` and `pnpm test` make the link first ([`tools/layerfs-source.mjs`](tools/layerfs-source.mjs)); after changing `LAYERFS_SOURCE`, run `pnpm run link:layerfs` (pnpm skips its install step when nothing else changed). The pin is LayerFS [v1.1.0](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/releases/tag/v1.1.0) (`9f97a7ec95`, on LayerFS `main`). Check out that tag in `../layerfs`, or set `LAYERFS_SOURCE` to a checkout of it. ### What stayed in the layerfs repository The demo bundle (disabled permanently, owner 2026-10-21), the demo tools (`demo.mjs`, `check-demo.mjs`, `check-scenario.mjs`), `init-project.mjs`, and the #352 history replay harness (`tools/history/`, `run-scenario`, `restore-store`, `import-run`) stayed in the layerfs repository; it measures LayerFS builds, not the plugin. Making the profile by hand is the same: that `package.json`, then `pnpm install` in the profile folder. Keep the `pnpm-workspace.yaml` dsh writes there (`nodeLinker: hoisted`), so the bundle shares dsh's own packages. ### 4. Configure Live The Host reads its deployment settings from `layerfs-host` in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` ([`config.js`](packages/host/src/config.js)). dsh writes that file as `[]`; replace the `[]` with the entry list below. | Setting | Linux | macOS | |---|---|---| | `image` | required | required | | `daemon` | required | defaults to `/layerfs-daemon` | | `bundle` | not used | required | | `docker` | `/var/run/docker.sock` by default | the same | | `volumes` | `/var/lib/docker/volumes` by default (Docker's data-root); the Host's user must write it | not used | | `home`, `traceDir` | `/dsh-layerfs/{home,traces}` by default | the same | | `containerPrefix` | `layerfs-` by default: Sandboxes `-` | the same, and the worker `worker` | | `stateDir` | `/dsh-layerfs` by default (bindings, agent names, journals) | the same | An Init without the required settings is refused with "LayerFS is not configured: set … for layerfs-host in the profile patch"; `GET /layerfs/status` lists what is `missing`. ```yaml # $DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml - id: layerfs-host config: image: "sha256:<64 hex>" # step 1's image ID bundle: /Users//layerfs-build # macOS: step 1's sealed bundle (manifest.json) # daemon: /path/to/layerfs-daemon # Linux ``` **On macOS** the Mac runs no Store call itself. `@layerfs/runtime` runs one long-lived Linux container per LayerFS home, the worker (`worker`, `layerfs-worker` by default, labelled `layerfs.role=worker`), and every Store call of the Host and of agents' scripts runs there with the sealed bundle's `layerfs.node`; its endpoint is `/worker/endpoint.json`, and agents get it as `DSH_LAYERFS_WORKER_ENDPOINT`. The Host starts it when it starts; a worker of another build is replaced, so load a new `bundle` only while no dsh run is live. It runs with `--restart unless-stopped`. A call of the Host or an agent that finds it down keeps its own error, and the Host asks the runtime to start it again. **On Linux** the Host and agents' scripts load `@layerfs/agent` in their own process, from `api/agent/sdk` in the LayerFS checkout (through `.layerfs`). It loads the addon from `LAYERFS_NATIVE`, or else `api/binding/layerfs.node`: build it on that machine with `npm --prefix "$LAYERFS_SOURCE/api" run build:native` ([SDK README](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/blob/main/api/README.md#builds-and-compatibility); it needs Cargo 1.85.1 on the host), or set `LAYERFS_NATIVE` in dsh web's environment to a Linux build's `layerfs.node`. `daemon` is that build's `layerfs-daemon`. The Store must be on a local Linux filesystem (ext4, xfs or btrfs). Init installs the Store straight into the new project's volume directory under Docker's volumes directory (`volum… **On Windows** dsh web and the default profile remain on Windows. `@layerfs/runtime` starts one long-lived Node worker in a selected WSL2 distribution, owned by the Host through its stdin. That distribution needs its own running Docker Engine, `/dev/fuse`, Node 22.19 or newer, and a **sealed Linux bundle** from `tools/worktree.py build` (run the build inside WSL, using the private resources described above). Docker Desktop's Windows named pipe is not used by this adapter. Install and build the plugin on Windows with steps 2–3. You can add it to your existing default `web` profile; omit the example's `DSH_HOME` override to do so. Keep that profile's existing patch entries and add: ```yaml - id: layerfs-host config: image: "sha256:" bundle: /home//layerfs-build # sealed Linux bundle, including manifest.json wslDistribution: Ubuntu # wslUser: root # default; must access Docker and its Store volumes # wslNode: /usr/local/bin/node # default; absolute Linux executable path # wslHome: /var/lib/dsh-layerfs-windows/my-profile containerPrefix: layerfs-windows- ``` `daemon` defaults to `/layerfs-daemon`. `bundle`, `daemon`, `wslNode`, and `wslHome` are Linux paths in that distribution. `home`, `traceDir`, and `stateDir` remain Windows paths. The default Linux home is a persistent directory under `/var/lib/dsh-layerfs-windows`, derived from the Windows home. Stores live in the WSL Docker Engine's named volumes on its local Linux filesystem. Never put the Store or Linux discovery home on `/mnt/c` or another Windows-backed mount. The Windows SDK entry preserves the regular SDK API for Host clients and agents. It forwards native calls to the worker; the product SDK and daemon are unchanged. Imports translate drive paths with that distribution's `wslpath`; WSL UNC paths must name the selected distribution. Init reads everything through the Linux filesystem view, including `.git` and ignored files. Windows ACLs are not converted to POSIX metadata; imported metadata is what WSL exposes. The worker validates the sealed bundle's file hashes, listens only on Linux loopback, and requires a random secret delivered over its startup pipe. Its Windows endpoint file is ACL-restricted to the current Windows user and SYSTEM. The Windows SDK source must match the sealed Linux SDK (allowing Git line-ending normalization). Windows binding-file readers share the writers' short admission lock so reads cannot overlap atomic file replacement; failed writes are not retried. Each project's native Store stays open while used and closes after a quiet minute. Project removal explicitly releases its cached Store before deleting the volume. Disposal drains admitted calls without killing mounted commands. Runtime Start and confirmed Restart act on this worker; a silent or busy worker is retained. Changing WSL deployment settings requires restarting dsh. The Host adds its Windows `layerfs.cmd` launcher to dsh's PATH. In a LayerFS-bound session, PowerShell and Command Prompt accept the same CLI commands as macOS, for example `layerfs project list_branches`. The launcher uses the session's `DSH_LAYERFS_CLI` wrapper and preserves stdin and exit codes. Shell syntax still follows the selected shell: PowerShell uses `$env:NAME`, not Bash's `$NAME`, and Bash heredocs are not PowerShell commands. SDK scenarios launch native Node scripts from the Scenarios workspace on Windows. CLI scenarios use a native runner for their limited command notation: quoted arguments, variables, substitutions, literal heredoc input, JSON field selection and tee. Each LayerFS operation invokes the real CLI wrapper; commands inside Linux Workspaces run unchanged. This runner is specific to scripted tests, not a Bash shell for arbitrary agent commands. Linux fixture files check out with LF even when Windows Git uses `core.autocrlf=true`. The dedicated `layerfs-scenarios` preset disables promotion of timed-out foreground commands to background jobs. Windows scripted calls have a 120-second dsh deadline; a 110-second watchdog attempts earlier cancellation. Captured CLI input/output uses temporary files because restricted Windows tokens deny Node named pipes. Explicit background steps keep their normal job ownership. Shipped scenarios use the configured Host image. The runtime Dockerfile includes Rust 1.85.1, SQLite development headers and Chromium/Selenium for Depot, alongside Node and the prepared package managers. Rebuild the image and configure its exact image ID when upgrading from the earlier Node-only image. Every scenario run creates a fresh project and retains earlier projects until explicit cleanup. Adapter or child failures immediately mark the run failed. `pnpm run test:scenarios` checks loading, launchers, fixtures and failure reporting; `node packages/host/tests/windows-cli.mjs` checks the Windows CLI launcher. For later Windows upgrades, keep the Windows checkout and WSL sealed bundle at the same `layerfs.json` pin, rebuild the runtime image when its Dockerfile changes, and run `check:layerfs`, `test:windows` and `test:scenarios` with a 120-second wall limit before live verification. A Cargo download timeout is a network failure: check registry access from the configured Sandbox image. This machine's optional [proxy deployment](docs/windows-live-20261024/deployment/README.md) records its network prerequisites; its addresses are not Windows defaults. WSL, Docker and any configured upstream proxy must be available before starting a run. A request lost before it is sent is `Failed`; a sent request whose reply is lost is `Unknown` and is never replayed. Failed Windows Init attempts retain their volume and Linux discovery state, with the original failure and volume recorded in `windows-init-failures.jsonl` under `stateDir`. Inspect that evidence before deciding how to recover. The macOS container adapter and Windows WSL adapter share the worker codec, but keep separate deployment and lifecycle code. The codec is versioned JSON with explicit binary values, independent of V8 serialization versions. Upgrade the Host and worker together, with no active calls; old V8 workers are incompatible and must be restarted. A protocol failure is reported explicitly and never replays a call. An uncertain Init reply also retains the macOS home and volume, recorded in `init-failures.jsonl` under `stateDir`, so protocol errors cannot trigger deletion of a completed Init. This setup uses the repository pnpm workspace and a dsh source checkout. Packaged dsh desktop and npm/plugin-market installation are not qualified ([#406](https://github.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/issues/406)). It ships in the bundle switched on, with this checkout's `scenarios/`; turn `@dsh-layerfs/mock` off on dsh's Plugins page to hide it. Off, nothing of it shows. A run picks its scenario's model on its own Session; dsh would save that pick as the default model for new Sessions, so the plugin keeps scripted models off the default and every other folder keeps your own. - **Scenarios** live in [`scenarios/`](scenarios/), one folder each with a `scenario.json` (loader and full format: [`packages/mock/src/scenario.js`](packages/mock/src/scenario.js)). Every step is one tool call of the minimalist preset (bash, subagent, send_message, the job tools) or a reply, written as an agent would type it. A scenario has one form, its first tag: in a `cli` scenario every bash step is plain `layerfs …` lines; in an `sdk` one every bash step is one inline Node script on the SDK. Half the scenarios are each: `cli` for shop, crew, parallel, checkpoints and conflicts; `sdk` for depot, tour, sandbox, agents and merge. A step that runs commands creates its own Sandbox, mounts one Workspace, runs, commits, unmounts and closes the Sandbox. - **Placeholders.** `{{scenario}}` (the folder's absolute path, written in double quotes) and `{{image}}` (the scenario's runtime image) are filled when it loads. `{{sandbox}}` and `{{commit:}}` are filled when the scripted model sends the step, from what that agent has seen: the last Sandbox number, and the Commit id a step with `commits: []` printed or a received message carried. A Commit id reaches another agent in a `send_message`. - **Checked while it runs.** A bash step's `expect` lists the LayerFS outcome codes its trace lines must show (`workspace.exec:exit:0`, `workspace.commit:Committed|UpToDate`, `workspace.commit:Conflict`), and `exit` its exit status (default 0). Before the agent's next step the scripted model reads the call's trace lines from the Host (its `layerfsTraces` service) and stops the run at the first mismatch. Commands carry no assertions of their own. - **Tags** (`cli`/`sdk`; `node`/`rust` where real builds run; one to three of `conflicts`, `merge`, `publish`, `multi-agent`, `background`, `sandbox`) show as chips on the Tests tab, which filters by them; the loader refuses an unknown tag and also counts each scenario's agents, steps and the LayerFS calls its `expect` checks. - **Replays** (`shop`, `depot`, `crew`) are recorded runs of real agents (layerfs #334, #337, #340) in this format: recorded writes are applied from `changes/` and recorded commands run again in Workspaces. [`tools/replay/convert.mjs`](tools/replay/convert.mjs) generates each folder from the recording at layerfs `0c7d9c47c1^`; rerun it rather than editing by hand, and see each folder's `CONVERSION.md` for what it kept and dropped. Their fixture is the recorded `seed.json` (it holds a `.git/HEAD`, which cannot live here as a file); the plugin writes it out to `/dsh-layerfs-mock/seeds//` when it loads. - **Checking a folder**: `node tools/replay/check.mjs ` loads it and parses every command (`bash -n`, or `node --check` for an SDK script) without running it. - **Checking a finished run**: `node tools/checks/run.mjs ` (the profile is `/profiles/web`) loads the scenario the run played, reads the Host's trace lines for the root and its subagents, and checks the run's state and every `expect`. A recorded `final.json` beside the scenario is reported as not checked: the order and final-tree checks ([`tools/checks/`](tools/checks/)) need a LayerFS client on the project. - **The Tests tab** on the LayerFS page lists every scenario with its latest run. Run all queues every scenario and runs up to 2 at once; each row has Run or Stop. A failed run shows why and keeps its project; Clean up removes the scenario projects no run is using. - **The Run bar** sits above a run's composer: Stop or Run again, and "Step n of m · phase" with a thin bar. - **Each run** gets a new Session in the Scenarios workspace (`/dsh-layerfs-mock/Scenarios`) and its own project, `mock-`, removed and Inited again from the scenario's fixture. The standalone HTML pages that used to live in the root `sdk_sim/` (the terminal UI page and its design preview) and their live server are removed; do not build or revive a standalone HTML or TUI page.
