# Let AI Agents Use Real Tools Safely

AgentFS provides isolated filesystem access backed by a SQLite file so agents can safely run the CLI tools they were trained on.

[Get Started](#getting-started) curl -fsSL https://agentfs.ai/install | bash

[video](https://hebbkx1anhila5yf.public.blob.vercel-storage.com/agentfs-demo%20%281%29-oS0G4u6bu1L5axiALeg6swuhUiwFpB.mp4)

Your browser does not support the video tag.

## Power vs. Safety

AI agents need filesystem access to be useful, but giving them full access is risky

### Agents Need Power

- •Access CLI tools and binaries
- •Read and modify project files
- •Run complex development workflows
- •Interact with tools and scripts
- •Resume execution from saved state

### But Access is Risky

- •Agents are inherently unpredictable
- •Accidental file deletion or corruption
- •No audit trail of what changed
- •Difficult to test and debug safely
- •Sessions are not resumable

AgentFS bridges this gap by providing resumable, isolated, auditable filesystem access that keeps your files safe while giving agents the tools they need

## Beyond Network Filesystems

Network filesystems work for traditional use cases, but the agentic world demands a different approach. AgentFS addresses three critical limitations.

### Billions of Filesystems

Network filesystems provide one shared mount, but infrastructure cannot sustain billions of individual mounts per agent.

AgentFS Solution

Each filesystem is a SQLite file. Store billions on any media.

### Instant Snapshots

Network filesystems require complex mechanisms to snapshot and rollback entire filesystem state.

AgentFS Solution

Single SQLite file enables instant snapshots and rollback.

### Effortless Forking

Network filesystems make copying entire hierarchies slow and complex when agents need to fork for subagents.

AgentFS Solution

SQLite files copy instantly for effortless forking.

AgentFS stores each filesystem as a SQLite file, giving you all the isolation benefits above. Sync them across agents however you want. Turso Cloud offers a turnkey solution, turning SQLite files into networked filesystems backed by S3.

## Built on Three Core Principles

AgentFS provides enterprise-grade safety for AI agents

Isolation

Copy-on-write overlay keeps original files untouched

AgentFS creates an isolated filesystem layer where all changes happen. Your original files remain completely safe and unchanged until you decide to apply the modifications.

Auditability

Every operation logged to a portable SQLite file

## README

# AppFS

Filesystem-native app protocol for shell-first AI agents, powered by AgentFS.

[中文 README](README.zh-CN.md)

AppFS turns different apps into one filesystem contract so agents can use the same primitives everywhere:

- `cat` to read resources
- `>> *.act` to trigger actions with JSONL
- `tail -f` to watch async event streams

This repository contains the AppFS protocol docs, runtime, reference fixtures, bridge adapters, and conformance tests. AppFS is the app-facing protocol and managed runtime; AgentFS is the storage, overlay, sync, and mount engine underneath.

## Overview

AppFS is designed for practical LLM + shell workflows:

- one interaction model across many apps instead of one schema per app
- path-native operations with low token overhead
- stream-first async flows with replay support
- managed runtime lifecycle with dynamic app registration
- connector adapters for in-process, HTTP, and gRPC integrations

## Powered by AgentFS

AppFS is the primary product story in this repository, but it is currently shipped through the AgentFS engine and CLI:

- `agentfs init ...` prepares the underlying AgentFS database and storage layer
- `agentfs appfs up ...` starts the managed AppFS runtime on top of that AgentFS-backed filesystem
- the `agentfs` binary remains the entrypoint because AppFS currently depends on AgentFS database lifecycle, overlay semantics, sync support, and platform mount backends

In other words: AppFS is the app-facing protocol and UX; AgentFS is the engine that powers it.

The recommended integration entrypoint for real app projects is:

```bash
agentfs appfs compose up -f appfs-compose.yaml
```

The lower-level managed runtime primitive remains:

```bash
agentfs appfs up <id-or-path> <mountpoint>
```

Managed runtime state lives in:

```text
/_appfs/apps.registry.json
```

Low-level debug commands still exist:

- `agentfs mount ... --managed-appfs`
- `agentfs serve appfs --managed`

## Quick Start

The higher-level AppFS flow is now:

1. declare runtime, connectors, and apps in `appfs-compose.yaml`
2. run `agentfs appfs compose up`
3. use the mounted tree directly

The lower-level managed flow is still:

1. start a bridge or in-process connector
2. initialize an empty AgentFS database that AppFS will use as its storage and mount substrate
3. start AppFS with `agentfs appfs up`
4. register an app through `/_appfs/register_app.act`
5. read files, switch scope, and trigger actions through the mounted tree

Today the recommended integration path is compose-first. `agentfs appfs up` remains the lower-level runtime primitive when you want to debug mount/runtime behavior directly.

A Huoyan attached-case compose example lives at [examples/appfs/appfs-compose.huoyan-attached-case.example.yaml](./examples/appfs/appfs-compose.huoyan-attached-case.example.yaml).

Minimal compose shape for the reference HTTP bridge:

```yaml
version: 1

runtime:
  db: ./.agentfs/compose-aiim.db
  mountpoint: C:/mnt/appfs-compose-aiim
  backend: winfsp
  init: if_missing
  reset: false
  fallback_poll_ms: 0

connectors:
  aiim-http:
    mode: command
    transport: http
    endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8080
    healthcheck:
      kind: connector
      interval_ms: 500
      timeout_ms: 2000
      max_attempts: 40
    command:
      cwd: ./examples/appfs/bridges/http-python
      program: uv
      args: ["run", "python", "bridge_server.py"]

apps:
  aiim:
    connector: aiim-http
```

Runtime polling is split by responsibility:

- `.act` writes are normally processed through the mount runtime's write-wake path, so action execution does not require polling.
- `apps.<app-id>.inbound_poll_ms` enables connector inbound event polling for apps that must pull backend-side events into the mounted tree, such as a chat inbox.
- `runtime.fallback_poll_ms` is a legacy full-runtime fallback tick. It is disabled by default and should usually stay `0`. The old compose field `runtime.poll_ms` and CLI flag `--poll-ms` are still accepted as compatibility aliases, but new configs should use `fallback_poll_ms`.

Private, principal-aware apps can be declared through app policy fields. Compose writes the policy/template, but the actual private instances are materialized when a principal is attached or created. For example, a Tinode app can materialize one private tree per AppFS principal and poll backend events into each tree:

```yaml
apps:
  tinode:
    connector: tinode-http
    visibility: private
    path_template: private/{principal_id}/tinode
    profile_template: tinode:{principal_id}
    credential_policy: auto-create
    inbound_poll_ms: 1000
```

That inbound poll keeps the mounted AppFS tree current. It does not replace a higher-level agent wake/subscription mechanism; agents still need to observe or read the relevant files until an explicit wake layer is added. In practice, the current identity and private app set are established by the appfs-agent attach flow, not by AppFS startup alone.

With that file in place:

```bash
agentfs appfs compose up -f appfs-compose.yaml
```

Compose is the recommended path when you want one command to:

- prepare or reopen the AgentFS runtime database
- supervise an external or command-launched connector
- bootstrap the managed AppFS registry
- mount the tree and start the runtime in one foreground process

Prerequisites:

- Rust toolchain with `cargo`
- Python + `uv` for the reference HTTP bridge
- port `127.0.0.1:8080` available
- Windows: WinFsp installed
- Linux: FUSE available
- macOS: NFS mount support available

## 找到的 Windows 原生项目

| 项目 | 做法 | 状态 |
|---|---|---|
| [**lane**](https://github.com/adamblumoff/lane)(Rust) | 自称 **"Windows-first"**:Codex skill + CLI,每个 agent 跑在一个 **WinFsp 挂载的 lane view** 里;按**单个文件操作**捕获变更(不是整树 diff),`lane run --attempts 5` 起 5 条并行 lane,`lane review/accept` 逐操作审查、冲突可用替换字节解决 | pre-alpha,0 star,目前只支持 Windows |
| [**appfs**](https://github.com/esp3j0/appfs)(Rust,基于 AgentFS 引擎) | Turso AgentFS 血统，叠加“文件系统即 app 协议”层(`cat` 读资源、`>> *.act` 触发动作);**Windows 用 `backend: winfsp` 挂载**，仓库里有 `cli/TEST-WINDOWS.md` 和完整 Windows 安装说明 | 个人项目，8 stars |
| 对照：主线 [tursodatabase/agentfs](https://www.agentfs.ai/) | 官方跨平台矩阵只有 Browser(OPFS)/ Linux(FUSE)/ macOS(NFS),**没有 Windows** | — |
| 对照：LayerFS / Phantom / try / agentvfs | 全部 Linux/macOS,Windows 一律 WSL 或不支持 | — |

## 为什么“都是 FUSE”

这个品类的统一架构是：**用户态存储引擎(SQLite/对象库)+ 一个把它呈现为真实目录的内核桥**。桥在哪个 OS 上是什么：

- **Linux**:只有 FUSE 这一个非特权用户态文件系统接口，所以全员 FUSE;内核 overlayfs 还要求 root 或 userns(Phantom/try 才能用)。
- **macOS**:macFUSE 是第三方内核扩展，所以 AgentFS 干脆用 localhost **NFS** 绕开。
- **Windows**:桥其实有**两座**，只是没人来走——

| | [WinFsp](https://winfsp.dev/rel/) | [ProjFS(Windows Projected File System)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/projfs/projected-file-system) |
|---|---|---|
| 定位 | 社区事实标准“Windows 版 FUSE”(rclone、SSHFS-Win、Cryptomator 都靠它) | 微软官方内核投影文件系统，VFS for Git / [Scalar](https://github.blog/open-source/git/the-story-of-scalar/) 用过，GitHub 还有 [libprojfs](https://github.com/github/libprojfs) |
| 模型 | 你实现完整文件系统，读写都归你 | **提供方按需投影内容**(placeholder + hydration),写落到 NTFS 真实文件——是“虚拟工作树”，不是 overlay |
| 代价 | 要装一个签名驱动(安装包一键) | 系统组件免安装，但写路径不被拦截，做 CoW 隔离要自己另想办法 |

所以上面两个 Windows 项目都选 WinFsp:这个品类需要的是“读投影 + 写捕获”，WinFsp 的模型对得上，ProjFS 的模型对不上(它解决的是 300GB monorepo 不想全 checkout 的问题，不是写隔离)。

## 为什么 Windows 原生这么少

1. **agent 基础设施本身偏向 Linux/macOS**:harness、容器、CI 全在 Linux,做工具的人顺手就写了 FUSE。
2. **NTFS 没有内核级 union/CoW 挂载**：Linux 上 `try`/Phantom 可以直接白嫖 overlayfs(内核帮你 CoW),Windows 上没有等价物——VSS 是只读卷快照，ReFS 的块 CoW 不暴露成可挂载层。于是 Windows 方案必须写一个**完整的用户态文件系统**，工程量直接上一个大台阶。
3. **WinFsp 要装驱动**：分发摩擦 > WSL2 一把梭，于是 LayerFS 这类项目算完账都选了 WSL。
4. 语义坑(上一轮说过)：大小写不敏感、ACL≠POSIX mode,做通用 agent FS 还得自己定契约。

结论：Windows 原生路线 = **WinFsp + 用户态引擎**，已被 lane 和 appfs 验证可行，但都还是个人/pre-alpha 级别。等哪个头部 harness(LayerFS、AgentFS 或 Claude Code 生态)认真要 Windows 支持，WinFsp 就是那个标准落点。

**Why FUSE-dominant**: Linux is where agents run (containers/CI/devboxes); FUSE is the only unprivileged-ish userland FS interface on Linux; the FS engine is userland (SQLite etc.) so it needs *some* kernel bridge; macOS substitutes NFS; Windows has its own bridges — WinFsp (community de-facto, used by rclone/SSHFS-Win/Cryptomator) and ProjFS/CfApi (Microsoft official, placeholder/projection model, used by VFS for Git).

**Windows options**:
- WinFsp = the Windows FUSE analog — GPL3+FLOSS exception, stable, signed driver. Projects using it for agents: lane (Windows-first), appfs (agentfs engine with winfsp backend).
- ProjFS = official but different model (projection/read-mostly, hydration; writes go to disk — it's a "projected" working tree, not an overlay. Writes land on NTFS; you track them yourself. VFS for Git used it for giant monorepos.)
- Also mention: no native union/overlay in NTFS (no overlayfs equivalent); VSS is read-only volume snapshots; ReFS CoW not exposed as mounts. So every Windows solution must be a full userland FS via WinFsp/ProjFS rather than kernel overlayfs composition. Also case sensitivity, ACL vs POSIX again.

Also mention Lane in detail since it's the direct Windows-native answer: file-level isolation, per-operation capture, `lane run --attempts N` = N parallel attempts in mounted lane views, review/accept with conflict resolution at op level, `.lane` storage. Pre-alpha, 0 stars — ecosystem reality: Windows-native agent-FS is embryonic.

And appfs: Windows via WinFsp documented, TEST-WINDOWS.md exists, compose examples with `backend: winfsp`, `C:/mnt/...` mountpoints.

Also should note Docker/containerd on Windows does snapshotting via scratch VHDs — different mechanism (block-level), used by Windows containers. Not userland-FS.

Structure the answer:
1. 直接回答:有,但极少、很早期。两个找到的:lane(Windows-first,WinFsp)、appfs(AgentFS 系,WinFsp backend)。主线 AgentFS/LayerFS/Phantom 都不支持 Windows。
2. 为什么都 FUSE:品类架构都是"用户态引擎(SQLite/对象库)+ 内核桥",Linux 桥只有 FUSE;macOS 用 NFS 绕;Windows 的桥其实存在且有两个。
3. Windows 的两座桥对比表:WinFsp vs ProjFS(+ 为什么 NTFS 没有 overlayfs,所以不能像 Linux 那样"内核 union + bind mount"低配方案)。
4. 找到的 Windows 原生项目表。
5. 结论:为什么少——需求方(agent 框架)几乎都在 Linux/macOS 跑;WinFsp 要装驱动;_projfs 模型只投影不 overlay;所以大家都 WSL 了事。LayerFS 选 WSL 正是这个生态现状的缩影。

Keep it terse. Cite links.

content.text:
有，但凤毛麟角，而且都用 **WinFsp**(Windows 世界的 FUSE)——Windows 原生方案是存在的，只是这个品类整体还太年轻，主力全在 Linux/macOS。

## 找到的 Windows 原生项目

| 项目 | 做法 | 状态 |
|---|---|---|
| [**lane**](https://github.com/adamblumoff/lane)(Rust) | 自称 **"Windows-first"**:Codex skill + CLI,每个 agent 跑在一个 **WinFsp 挂载的 lane view** 里;按**单个文件操作**捕获变更(不是整树 diff),`lane run --attempts 5` 起 5 条并行 lane,`lane review/accept` 逐操作审查、冲突可用替换字节解决 | pre-alpha,0 star,目前只支持 Windows |
| [**appfs**](https://github.com/esp3j0/appfs)(Rust,基于 AgentFS 引擎) | Turso AgentFS 血统，叠加“文件系统即 app 协议”层(`cat` 读资源、`>> *.act` 触发动作);**Windows 用 `backend: winfsp` 挂载**，仓库里有 `cli/TEST-WINDOWS.md` 和完整 Windows 安装说明 | 个人项目，8 stars |
| 对照：主线 [tursodatabase/agentfs](https://www.agentfs.ai/) | 官方跨平台矩阵只有 Browser(OPFS)/ Linux(FUSE)/ macOS(NFS),**没有 Windows** | — |
| 对照：LayerFS / Phantom / try / agentvfs | 全部 Linux/macOS,Windows 一律 WSL 或不支持 | — |

## 为什么“都是 FUSE”

这个品类的统一架构是：**用户态存储引擎(SQLite/对象库)+ 一个把它呈现为真实目录的内核桥**。桥在哪个 OS 上是什么：

- **Linux**:只有 FUSE 这一个非特权用户态文件系统接口，所以全员 FUSE;内核 overlayfs 还要求 root 或 userns(Phantom/try 才能用)。
- **macOS**:macFUSE 是第三方内核扩展，所以 AgentFS 干脆用 localhost **NFS** 绕开。
- **Windows**:桥其实有**两座**，只是没人来走——

| | [WinFsp](https://winfsp.dev/rel/) | [ProjFS(Windows Projected File System)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/projfs/projected-file-system) |
|---|---|---|
| 定位 | 社区事实标准“Windows 版 FUSE”(rclone、SSHFS-Win、Cryptomator 都靠它) | 微软官方内核投影文件系统，VFS for Git / [Scalar](https://github.blog/open-source/git/the-story-of-scalar/) 用过，GitHub 还有 [libprojfs](https://github.com/github/libprojfs) |
| 模型 | 你实现完整文件系统，读写都归你 | **提供方按需投影内容**(placeholder + hydration),写落到 NTFS 真实文件——是“虚拟工作树”，不是 overlay |
| 代价 | 要装一个签名驱动(安装包一键) | 系统组件免安装，但写路径不被拦截，做 CoW 隔离要自己另想办法 |

所以上面两个 Windows 项目都选 WinFsp:这个品类需要的是“读投影 + 写捕获”，WinFsp 的模型对得上，ProjFS 的模型对不上(它解决的是 300GB monorepo 不想全 checkout 的问题，不是写隔离)。

## 为什么 Windows 原生这么少

1. **agent 基础设施本身偏向 Linux/macOS**:harness、容器、CI 全在 Linux,做工具的人顺手就写了 FUSE。
2. **NTFS 没有内核级 union/CoW 挂载**：Linux 上 `try`/Phantom 可以直接白嫖 overlayfs(内核帮你 CoW),Windows 上没有等价物——VSS 是只读卷快照，ReFS 的块 CoW 不暴露成可挂载层。于是 Windows 方案必须写一个**完整的用户态文件系统**，工程量直接上一个大台阶。
3. **WinFsp 要装驱动**：分发摩擦 > WSL2 一把梭，于是 LayerFS 这类项目算完账都选了 WSL。
4. 语义坑(上一轮说过)：大小写不敏感、ACL≠POSIX mode,做通用 agent FS 还得自己定契约。

结论：Windows 原生路线 = **WinFsp + 用户态引擎**，已被 lane 和 appfs 验证可行，但都还是个人/pre-alpha 级别。等哪个头部 harness(LayerFS、AgentFS 或 Claude Code 生态)认真要 Windows 支持，WinFsp 就是那个标准落点。

# WinFsp

# WinFsp Performance Testing

This document presents results from performance testing of WinFsp. These results show that WinFsp has excellent performance that rivals or exceeds that of NTFS in many file system scenarios. Some further optimization opportunities are also identified.

## Summary

Two reference WinFsp file systems, MEMFS and NTPTFS, are compared against NTFS in multiple file system scenarios. MEMFS is an in-memory file system, whereas NTPTFS (NT passthrough file system) is a file system that passes all file system requests onto an underlying NTFS file system.

The test results are summarized in the charts below. The "File Tests" chart summarizes performance of file path namespace manipulations (e.g. creating/deleting files, opening files, listing files, etc.). The "Read/Write Tests" chart summarizes performance of file I/O (e.g. cached read/write, memory mapped I/O, etc.)

The important takeaways are:

- MEMFS is faster than NTFS is most scenarios. This is a somewhat expected result because MEMFS is an in-memory file system, whereas NTFS is a disk file system. However it shows that WinFsp does not add significant overhead and user mode file systems can be fast.

- MEMFS and NTPTFS both outperform NTFS when doing cached file I/O! This is a significant result because doing file I/O is the primary purpose of a file system. It is also an unexpected result at least in the case of NTPTFS, since NTPTFS runs on top of NTFS.

The following sections present the testing methodology used, provide instructions for independent verification, describe the individual tests in detail and provide an explanation for the observed results.

| ![file tests](file_tests.png) | ![rdwr tests](rdwr_tests.png) |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- |

## Methodology

A test run consists of performance tests run one after the other (in sequence). The test driver is careful to clear system caches before each test to minimize timing interference between the tests (because we would not want operations performed in test A to affect measurements of test B). Tests are run on an idle computer to minimize interference from third party components.

Each test run is run a number of times (default: 3) against each file system and the smallest time value for the particular test and file system is chosen. The assumption is that even in a seemingly idle system there is some activity that affects the results; the smallest value is the preferred one to use because it reflects the time when there is less or no other system activity.

For the NTFS file system we use the default configuration as it ships with Windows (e.g. 8.3 names are enabled). For the NTPTFS file system we disable anti-virus checks on the lower file system, because it makes no sense for NTPTFS to pay for virus checking twice. (Consider an NTPTFS file system that exposes a lower NTFS directory `C:\t` as an upper drive `X:`. Such a file system would have virus checking applied on file accesses to `X:`, but also to its own accesses to `C:\t`. This is unnecessary and counter-productive.)

Note that the sequential nature of the tests represents a worst case scenario for WinFsp. The reason is that a single file system operation may require a roundtrip to the user mode file system and such a roundtrip requires two process context switches (i.e. address space and thread switches): one context switch to carry the file system request to the user mode file system and one context switch to carry the response back to the originating process. WinFsp performs better when multiple processes issue file system operations concurrently, because multiple requests are queued in its internal queues and multiple requests can be handled in a single context switch.

For more information refer to the [Performance Testing Analysis](WinFsp-Performance-Testing-Analysis.ipynb) notebook. This notebook together with the `run-all-perf-tests.bat` script can be used for replication and independent verification of the results presented in this document.

The test environment for the results presented in this document is as follows:

```
Dell XPS 13 9300
Intel Core i7-1065G7 CPU
32GB 3733MHz LPDDR4x RAM
2TB M.2 PCIe NVMe SSD

Windows 11 (64-bit) Version 21H2 (OS Build 22000.258)
WinFsp 2022+ARM64 Beta3 (v1.11B3)
```

## Results

In the charts below we use consistent coloring and markers to quickly identify a file system. Blue and the letter 'N' is used for NTFS, orange and the letter 'M' is used for MEMFS, green and the letter 'P' is used for NTPTFS.

In bar charts shorter bars are better. In plot charts lower times are better. (Better means that the file system is faster).

### File Tests

File tests are tests that are performed against the hierarchical path namespace of a file system. These tests measure the performance of creating, opening, overwriting, listing and deleting files.

Measured times for these tests are normalized against the NTFS time (so that the NTFS value is always 1). This allows for easy comparison between file systems across all file tests.

MEMFS has the best performance in most of these tests. NTFS performs better in some tests; these are discussed further below. NTPTFS is last as it has the overhead of both NTFS and WinFsp.

![file tests](file_tests.png)

#### file_create_test

This test measures the performance of creating new files using `CreateFileW(CREATE_NEW)` / `CloseHandle`. MEMFS has the best performance here, while NTFS has worse performance as it has to update its data structures on disk.

![file create test](file_create_test.png)

#### file_open_test

This test measures the performance of opening different files using `CreateFileW(OPEN_EXISTING)` / `CloseHandle`. MEMFS again has the best performance, followed by NTFS and then NTPTFS.

![file open test](file_open_test.png)

#### iter.file_open_test

This test measures the performance of opening the same files repeatedly using `CreateFileW(OPEN_EXISTING)` / `CloseHandle`. NTFS has the best performance, with MEMFS following and NTPTFS a distant third.

This test shows that NTFS does a better job than WinFsp when re-opening a file. The problem is that in most cases the WinFsp API design requires a round-trip to the user mode file system when opening a file. Improving WinFsp performance here would likely require substantial changes to the WinFsp API.

![iter.file open test](iter.file_open_test.png)

#### file_overwrite_test

This test measures the performance of overwriting files using `CreateFileW(CREATE_ALWAYS)` / `CloseHandle`. MEMFS is fastest, followed by NTFS and then NTPTFS.

![file overwrite test](file_overwrite_test.png)

#### file_list_test

This test measures the performance of listing files using `FindFirstFileW` / `FindNextFile` / `FindClose`. MEMFS is again fastest with NTFS and NTPTFS following.

It should be noted that NTFS can perform better in this test, if 8.3 (i.e. short) names are disabled (see `fsutil 8dot3name`). However Microsoft ships NTFS with 8.3 names enabled by default and these tests are performed against the default configuration of NTFS.

![file list test](file_list_test.png)

#### file_list_single_test

This test measures the performance of listing a single file using `FindFirstFileW` / `FindNextFile` / `FindClose`. NTFS has again best performance, with MEMFS following and NTPTFS a distant third.

This test shows that NTFS does a better job than WinFsp at caching directory data. Improving WinFsp performance here would likely require a more aggressive and/or intelligent directory caching scheme than the one used now.

![file list single test](file_list_single_test.png)

#### file_delete_test

This test measures the performance of deleting files using `DeleteFileW`. MEMFS has the best performance, followed by NTFS and NTPTFS.

![file delete test](file_delete_test.png)

### Read/Write Tests

Read/write tests are tests that measure the performance of cached, non-cached and memory-mapped I/O.

Measured times for these tests are normalized against the NTFS time (so that the NTFS value is always 1). This allows for easy comparison between file systems across all read/write tests.

MEMFS and NTPTFS outperform NTFS in cached and non-cached I/O tests and have equal performance to NTFS in memory mapped I/O tests. This result may be somewhat counter-intuitive (especially for NTPTFS), but the reasons are explained below.

![rdwr tests](rdwr_tests.png)

#### rdwr_cc_read_page_test

This test measures the performance of cached `ReadFile` with 1 page reads. MEMFS and NTPTFS outperform NTFS by a considerable margin.

Cached reads are satisfied from cache and they can effectively be a "memory copy" from the operating system’s buffers into the `ReadFile` buffer. Both WinFsp and NTFS implement NT "fast I/O" and one explanation for the test’s result is that the WinFsp "fast I/O" implementation is more performant than the NTFS one.

An alternative explanation is that MEMFS and NTPTFS are simply faster in filling the file system cache when a cache miss occurs. While this may be true for MEMFS (because it maintains file data in user mode memory), it cannot be true for NTPTFS. Recall that the test driver clears system caches prior to running every test, which means that when NTPTFS tries to fill its file system cache for the upper file system, it has to access lower file system data from disk (the same as NTFS).

![rdwr cc read page test](rdwr_cc_read_page_test.png)

#### rdwr_cc_write_page_test

This test measures the performance of cached `WriteFile` with 1 page writes. As in the read case, MEMFS and NTPTFS outperform NTFS albeit with a smaller margin.

Similar comments as for `rdwr_cc_read_page_test` apply.

![rdwr cc write page test](rdwr_cc_write_page_test.png)

#### rdwr_nc_read_page_test

This test measures the performance of non-cached `ReadFile` with 1 page reads. Although MEMFS and NTPTFS have better performance than NTFS, this result is not as interesting, because MEMFS is an in-memory file system and NTPTFS currently implements only cached I/O (this may change in the future). However we include this test for completeness.

![rdwr nc read page test](rdwr_nc_read_page_test.png)

#### rdwr_nc_write_page_test

This test measures the performance of non-cached `WriteFile` with 1 page writes. Again MEMFS and NTPTFS have better performance than NTFS, but similar comments as for `rdwr_nc_read_page_test` apply.

![rdwr nc write page test](rdwr_nc_write_page_test.png)

#### mmap_read_test

This test measures the performance of memory mapped reads. NTFS and WinFsp have identical performance here, which actually makes sense because memory mapped I/O is effectively cached by buffers that are mapped into the address space of the process doing the I/O.

![mmap read test](mmap_read_test.png)

#### mmap_write_test

This test measures the performance of memory mapped writes. NTFS and WinFsp have again identical performance here. Similar comments as for `mmap_read_test` apply.

![mmap write test](mmap_write_test.png)

meta-viewport: width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0
title: "Appendix: Approaches to Virtualized Working Trees | High Performance Git"
---

Sparse-checkout says: "do not materialize everything." Partial clone says: "do not download everything up front." A virtualized or projected working tree pushes the idea further — present the namespace now, fetch file content only when something actually reads it.

This appendix is about what lives outside stock Git. Virtualized working trees are a design pattern implemented by external tools — VFS for Git, GVFS protocol extensions, projected filesystem drivers — not a feature you turn on with `git config`. The approach shaped Git's large-repo roadmap, and the built-in features (sparse-checkout, partial clone, prefetch, Scalar) now cover most of the motivating use cases. It clarifies what the stock features are *not* doing.

---

## The Core Idea

A projected working tree keeps the directory listing more complete than the bytes on disk. The filesystem layer presents placeholders for files that have not been hydrated; opening one triggers a fetch.

That changes the local contract:

- the user sees paths that are not fully local
- editors, builds, and watchers can trigger hydration just by touching a path
- "listed file" and "fully present local file" stop being the same thing

The benefit is startup cost. First clone, branch switch, and initial materialization get much cheaper because the filesystem view is cheap to present. The cost is hydration latency and variability at access time, and a working tree that does not behave quite like a normal one.

## Where This Actually Runs

- **VFS for Git (Windows)**: Microsoft's original projected-filesystem Git, built around Windows' ProjFS. Superseded internally by Scalar plus stock Git features. No longer actively developed.
- **GVFS protocol extensions on servers**: custom endpoints that serve object content on narrow demand. Not part of stock Git; hosts implement them if at all.
- **Monorepo-specific systems**: some large organizations maintain internal projected filesystems on top of FUSE or platform-specific projection APIs. These are bespoke and do not usually ship as a generic Git plugin.

Stock `git` does not ship a virtualized working tree. There is no `git config core.projectedFilesystem`. If you want this behavior today, you are either on VFS for Git (legacy), using an internal tool, or approximating with the stack of built-in features below.

## The Built-In Stack Covers Most of the Same Ground

```sh
git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout <url> repo
cd repo
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set src docs
git checkout main
```

That sequence is the concrete approximation stock Git offers, well short of a true projected filesystem:

- `--filter=blob:none` defers object content until needed
- `--no-checkout` plus `sparse-checkout` narrows what gets written to disk
- lazy fetch handles the "I suddenly need this blob" case

You can see the namespace-versus-materialization split with ordinary commands:

```sh
git ls-files --sparse | sed -n '1,20p'
git show HEAD:path/to/file | head
test -e path/to/file || echo not materialized
```

Git can enumerate tracked paths and read content from the repository without those paths being present as local files. A real projected filesystem pushes that split further down, into the filesystem view itself.

## When the External Dependency Is Worth It

Virtualization makes sense when:

- the repo is very large
- most users touch a small fraction of the tree
- the namespace itself matters for navigation and tooling
- local disk is constrained
- hydration is fast and reliable

It does not make sense when:

- tools eagerly crawl the whole tree anyway
- offline work matters
- hydration latency is unpredictable
- the repo is large but user access is broad

For most teams, the built-in stack (sparse-checkout, sparse-index, partial clone, Scalar, `git maintenance`, `git backfill`) covers the same pressure without a projected filesystem. Virtualization still wins in a few places — mostly very large internal monorepos with skewed usage — but it is no longer the direction the ecosystem is moving in most ordinary cases.

The practical question for most readers is not "should I deploy a projected filesystem?" It is "how far can the built-in features take me before I would need one?" For most repos, further than you would think. When you need a VFS though, you'll know.

URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/VFSForGit/master/docs/faq.md
Content-Type: text/plain
Method: github-raw
Notes: Fetched raw: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/VFSForGit/master/docs/faq.md

---

Frequently Asked Questions
==========================

Here are some questions that users often have with VFS for Git, but are
unrelated to [troubleshooting issues](troubleshooting.md).

### Why does `gvfs clone` create a `<repo>/src` folder?

VFS for Git integrates with ProjFS to keep track of changes under this `src` folder.
Any activity in this folder is assumed to be important to Git operations. By
creating the `src` folder, we are making it easy for your build system to
create output folders outside the `src` directory. We commonly see systems
create folders for build outputs and package downloads. VFS for Git creates
these folders during its builds.

Your build system may create build artifacts such as `.obj` or `.lib` files
next to your source code. These are commonly "hidden" from Git using
`.gitignore` files. Having such artifacts in your source tree creates
additional work for Git because it needs to look at these files and match them
against the `.gitignore` patterns.

By following the pattern VFS for Git tries to establish and placing your build
intermediates and outputs parallel with the `src` folder and not inside it,
you can help optimize Git command performance for developers in the repository
by limiting the number of files Git needs to consider for many common
operations.

### Why the name change?

This project was formerly known as GVFS (Git Virtual File System). It is
undergoing a rename to VFS for Git. While the rename is in progress, the
code, protocol, built executables, and releases may still refer to the old
GVFS name. See https://github.com/Microsoft/VFSForGit/projects/4 for the
latest status of the rename effort.

### Why only Windows? Wasn't there a macOS version coming?

We were working hard to deliver a macOS version, and there are still many
remnants of that effort in the codebase. We were heavily dependent upon the
macOS KAUTH kernel extensions to provide equivalent functionality of ProjFS on
Windows. Unfortunately, [Apple deprecated this feature in Catalina](https://developer.apple.com/support/kernel-extensions/).
All of the recommended alternatives were either not appropriate for our
scenario or were not fast enough.

We transitioned our large repository strategy to focus on using
[`git sparse-checkout`](https://github.blog/2020-01-17-bring-your-monorepo-down-to-size-with-sparse-checkout/)
instead of filesystem virtualization. We then forked the VFS for Git
codebase to create [Scalar](https://github.com/microsoft/scalar). Those
investments in a cross-platform tool paid off since Scalar could launch
quickly.

### Why are you abandoning VFS for Git?

We will continue supporting VFS for Git as long as there is a need for it.
Through our experience, we have found that it is appropriate for only a very
small number of extremely large repos. For instance, the Windows OS repository
will depend on VFS for Git for the foreseeable future, and we will continue
supporting them. This includes updating VFS for Git with new versions of Git.

The basic issue with VFS for Git is that users who don’t know exactly what’s
going on will frequently get into bad states, such as populating too much of
their working directory or not properly enabling the ProjFS feature (this is
a larger problem for users using older versions of Windows). The Windows OS
team developed a lot of tribal knowledge for how to avoid known issues with
VFS for Git.

We prefer users adopting Scalar because that is where we are investing most
of our engineering efforts. The system is simpler and has a better “offramp”
onto core Git, if one decides that they want to get there. We are also
investing in making the Git client do more of the heavy lifting and reducing
how much is really a “Scalar” feature and how much is just a Git feature.

The FAQ doesn't have concrete perf numbers. I have enough to write a solid performance comparison. Let me also recall known concrete data points:

1. WinFsp official benchmarks (winfsp.dev/doc/WinFsp-Performance-Testing): MEMFS (in-memory FS through WinFsp) beats NTFS in most metadata ops (create/open/overwrite/list/delete); loses on repeated open (iter.file_open) and single-file listing (directory cache). Cached I/O (page read/write) faster than NTFS (fast I/O path); mmap identical. NTPTFS (passthrough over NTFS, worst case double stack) still beats NTFS on cached I/O but is last in metadata. Environment: i7-1065G7 laptop, Win11, WinFsp 1.11B3. Sequential tests = worst case for WinFsp because each op costs 2 context switches; concurrent loads amortize (batched dispatch).

2. Dokan comparison: WinFsp generally faster than Dokany (HN thread "faster than Dokany"; cppcryptfs research issue). Can mention as context — WinFsp is the fastest of the user-mode FS frameworks on Windows.

3. ProjFS performance profile:
   - Directory enumeration → provider callback per directory (GetPlaceholderInfo callbacks). VFS4G had to optimize enumeration heavily (projection-based folder counting PR #1917). Slow provider = slow dir listing.
   - First open of placeholder → hydration callback (network in VFS4G case) — high latency spikes at unpredictable times (gitperf: "hydration latency and variability at access time").
   - After hydration → real NTFS file: read/write = full native NTFS speed, zero framework overhead on the hot path.
   - Writes: go directly to NTFS, never intercepted → native speed, but no capture (that's the CoW problem stated earlier).
   - VFS4G's own perf claims (from blog posts/announcements): clone of 300GB Windows repo in ~10-20 min (vs hours), git status seconds. I shouldn't cite numbers I can't verify — the read didn't include them. I can state qualitatively: its goal was making 300GB Windows repo usable; gitperf quote covers qualitative.
   - Microsoft abandoned it: "users frequently get into bad states", "appropriate for only a very small number of extremely large repos", transitioned to sparse-checkout — perf wasn't the killer, operational complexity was.

4. For agent-FS use case (the frame of this whole conversation):
   - WinFsp: all reads/writes cross into userland engine (SQLite etc.) — the LayerFS/AgentFS model. WinFsp overhead is small (proven by MEMFS beating NTFS), but the engine's own cost dominates (SQLite lookups per op). Parallelism: WinFsp batches under concurrency — good for multi-agent.
   - ProjFS: fast after hydration but cannot intercept writes → can't implement the review-then-apply/CoW capture that defines the category. It solves read-side laziness only.
   - Also note: Defender double-scan issue (userland FS + backing store both scanned) — real-world WinFsp perf pitfall (noted in WinFsp doc re NTPTFS AV checks).

Structure: 
- 一句结论
- 机制决定性能模型(每操作跨界 vs 一次性水合后原生)
- WinFsp 实测数据(官方基准要点)
- ProjFS 性能剖面(枚举回调慢、水合延迟抖动、水合后原生、写原生)
- 针对 agent-FS 场景的判定表
- 注意事项(Defender 双扫、顺序 vs 并发、Dokan 对比、微软自己弃了 VFS4G)

Table format good. Keep citations.

content.text:
结论先行：**两者不是同一量级意义上的“文件系统性能”对比——WinFsp 的开销摊在每一次操作上(但实测很小，官方基准里多数场景打平甚至反超 NTFS);ProjFS 的开销集中在目录枚举和首次水合，之后就是纯 NTFS 原生速度，但代价是写路径完全不经过你**。

## 性能模型：机制决定的分工

| | WinFsp | ProjFS |
|---|---|---|
| 每次读/写 | 内核 ↔ 用户态引擎一次往返(2 次上下文切换) | 水合前：回调提供方；**水合后：直接读 NTFS,零框架开销** |
| 目录枚举 | 回调你的引擎 | 回调你的提供方(每个目录一次) |
| 写 | 全部进你的用户态引擎(可捕获) | **直接落 NTFS,不拦截**(所以快，也所以做不了 CoW) |
| 抖动来源 | 每操作恒定小开销 | 首次访问某个文件时的水合延迟尖峰(不可预测) |

## WinFsp 实测([官方基准](https://winfsp.dev/doc/WinFsp-Performance-Testing/),i7-1065G7 / Win11 / NVMe)

用两个参考文件系统对比 NTFS:MEMFS(纯内存 FS)、NTPTFS(穿透过 NTFS,最坏情况双重栈)：

- **元数据操作**(create/open/overwrite/list/delete):MEMFS **大多数项目快过 NTFS**(NTFS 要更新盘上数据结构)；NTPTFS 垫底但可接受(NTFS+WinFsp 双重开销)。
- **缓存 I/O**(页读/页写)：MEMFS 和 NTPTFS **双双快过原生 NTFS**——WinFsp 的 fast I/O 路径和缓存回填比 NTFS 自己的实现更高效，这是反直觉但可复现的结果。
- **mmap 读写：与 NTFS 完全持平**。
- **弱项**：重复打开同一文件(`iter.file_open`)和单文件目录列举——WinFsp 的目录缓存比 NTFS 弱，open 基本躲不开一次用户态往返，作者承认改进需要大改 API。
- **两个关键修饰**：① 测试是顺序单线程跑的，恰是 WinFsp **最坏情况**；并发时请求在内部队列聚合、一次上下文切换处理多个请求，多 agent 并发场景反而更占便宜。② 真实世界第一杀手不是 WinFsp 而是 **Defender 双重扫描**(挂载点和底层存储各扫一遍，官方文档专门为此关了 AV)。

顺带：WinFsp 也是 Windows 用户态 FS 框架里最快的——对比 Dokany,WinFsp 各项基准占优([HN 讨论](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=13126987)、[cppcryptfs 实测](https://github.com/bailey27/cppcryptfs/issues/18))。

## ProjFS 实测画像

没有等价的官方微基准，但工程结论一致：

- **水合后 = 原生 NTFS**:文件是真文件，读写、构建、编译器访问零开销——这是它对 WinFsp 的结构性优势。
- **枚举和水合是痛点**：每个目录列举、每个 placeholder 首开都要回调提供方。VFS for Git 为此做了大量优化(如 [用投影数据直接数目录](https://github.com/microsoft/VFSForGit/pull/1917) 以避免 `git ls-tree` 全量枚举)。
- **延迟不可预测**：访问时水合意味着任意一次 `open` 可能吃一次网络往返的尖峰——[gitperf 的总结](https://gitperf.com/appendix-virtualized-working-trees.html)原文:*"The cost is hydration latency and variability at access time, and a working tree that does not behave quite like a normal one"*,并点名“工具全树爬一遍就全水合了”(agent 的 grep/build 正是这种访问模式)。
- **微软自己的结局**:[FAQ](https://github.com/microsoft/VFSForGit/blob/master/docs/faq.md) 承认它"appropriate for only a very small number of extremely large repos",用户容易进入坏状态，主力转向 sparse-checkout/Scalar。死因是**运维复杂度**，不是吞吐。

## 对 agent 工作区这个场景的判定

| 需求 | 赢家 | 原因 |
|---|---|---|
| 写捕获/CoW/review-then-apply(品类定义) | **WinFsp,唯一选项** | ProjFS 写不经过你，根本拿不到变更流 |
| 全树读取(grep、build、tsc) | ProjFS(水合后) | 零框架开销；但 WinFsp 缓存 I/O 也只是略慢于 NTFS,且 MEMFS 级引擎可反超 |
| 大仓库首挂载/秒级 fork | ProjFS 理论强(placeholder 不带字节) | 但你的引擎若是 SQLite(LayerFS/AgentFS 模式)，WinFsp 侧同样免拷贝 |
| 多 agent 并发 | WinFsp | 队列聚合，并发下开销摊薄 |
| 延迟确定性 | WinFsp | 恒定小开销 vs 水合尖峰 |

一句话：**做 LayerFS 式的“agent 独立工作目录”，WinFsp 的性能税实测是 NTFS 同级(弱在重复 open 和目录缓存，强在缓存 I/O 和并发)，可接受；ProjFS 水合后更快，但它只解决“读得懒”，不解决“写得住”——对这个品类是功能缺失，不是性能权衡。**

- **两个关键修饰**：① 测试是顺序单线程跑的，恰是 WinFsp **最坏情况**；并发时请求在内部队列聚合、一次上下文切换处理多个请求，多 agent 并发场景反而更占便宜。② 真实世界第一杀手不是 WinFsp 而是 **Defender 双重扫描**(挂载点和底层存储各扫一遍，官方文档专门为此关了 AV)。

顺带：WinFsp 也是 Windows 用户态 FS 框架里最快的——对比 Dokany,WinFsp 各项基准占优([HN 讨论](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=13126987)、[cppcryptfs 实测](https://github.com/bailey27/cppcryptfs/issues/18))。

## ProjFS 实测画像

没有等价的官方微基准，但工程结论一致：

- **水合后 = 原生 NTFS**:文件是真文件，读写、构建、编译器访问零开销——这是它对 WinFsp 的结构性优势。
- **枚举和水合是痛点**：每个目录列举、每个 placeholder 首开都要回调提供方。VFS for Git 为此做了大量优化(如 [用投影数据直接数目录](https://github.com/microsoft/VFSForGit/pull/1917) 以避免 `git ls-tree` 全量枚举)。
- **延迟不可预测**：访问时水合意味着任意一次 `open` 可能吃一次网络往返的尖峰——[gitperf 的总结](https://gitperf.com/appendix-virtualized-working-trees.html)原文:*"The cost is hydration latency and variability at access time, and a working tree that does not behave quite like a normal one"*,并点名“工具全树爬一遍就全水合了”(agent 的 grep/build 正是这种访问模式)。
- **微软自己的结局**:[FAQ](https://github.com/microsoft/VFSForGit/blob/master/docs/faq.md) 承认它"appropriate for only a very small number of extremely large repos",用户容易进入坏状态，主力转向 sparse-checkout/Scalar。死因是**运维复杂度**，不是吞吐。

## 对 agent 工作区这个场景的判定

| 需求 | 赢家 | 原因 |
|---|---|---|
| 写捕获/CoW/review-then-apply(品类定义) | **WinFsp,唯一选项** | ProjFS 写不经过你，根本拿不到变更流 |
| 全树读取(grep、build、tsc) | ProjFS(水合后) | 零框架开销；但 WinFsp 缓存 I/O 也只是略慢于 NTFS,且 MEMFS 级引擎可反超 |
| 大仓库首挂载/秒级 fork | ProjFS 理论强(placeholder 不带字节) | 但你的引擎若是 SQLite(LayerFS/AgentFS 模式)，WinFsp 侧同样免拷贝 |
| 多 agent 并发 | WinFsp | 队列聚合，并发下开销摊薄 |
| 延迟确定性 | WinFsp | 恒定小开销 vs 水合尖峰 |

一句话：**做 LayerFS 式的“agent 独立工作目录”，WinFsp 的性能税实测是 NTFS 同级(弱在重复 open 和目录缓存，强在缓存 I/O 和并发)，可接受；ProjFS 水合后更快，但它只解决“读得懒”，不解决“写得住”——对这个品类是功能缺失，不是性能权衡。**
但是 winfsp 体积如何，可以user level 分发嘛

The user asks: WinFsp size, and can it be distributed at user level (no admin/installer)? Let me research facts:

Known facts about WinFsp:
- WinFsp is a kernel driver (winfsp.sys) + FSD launcher service (WinFsp.Launcher) + user-mode DLL. Installing requires admin (driver install). The MSI installer requires admin rights.
- Size: the MSI is roughly ~1.5-2 MB? Let me check. The WinFsp MSI is about 1.8 MB I believe. Actually winfsp releases: winfsp-2.1.25151.msi ~ 1.9 MB. Very small. Core package winfsp.sys is a few hundred KB.
- There is a "winfsp-noinstall" ZIP? Historically WinFsp provided testing "noinstall" builds? Let me verify. I recall there was a .zip for special cases. There is "winfsp-tests" separate. Hmm.
- Loading a kernel driver without admin: not possible normally. Driver installation needs admin (sc create / PnP install). Signing: WinFsp is WHQL/attestation signed, but loading still requires admin privileges. There's no user-mode-only fallback — the whole point is a kernel driver.
- Alternative: Dokan also needs admin driver install.
- ProjFS: the driver ships in-box with Windows 10 1809+; enabling the optional capability (`Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -FeatureName Client-ProjFS -Online` / `dism /online /enable-feature`) requires admin **once**; after enabling, using it (PrjStartVirtualizing) is user-mode, no admin needed per-mount. So ProjFS is "in-box but gated behind a one-time admin feature-enable".
- WinFsp distribution options: MSI (admin), also there's a "per-user"? No. But WinFsp has official support for "deployment via MSI with limited UI", enterprise deployment. Also worth noting: Cloudflare/WARP? no. rclone distributes WinFsp by prompting user to install. Cryptomator requires WinFsp installed with admin. SSHFS-Win bundles WinFsp installer.
- There is also a nuance: WinFsp offers "winfsp MSI" plus a "driver-only" merge module? There is a merge module (MSM) for embedding in app installers. Yes, winfsp provides an MSM merge module for OEM embedding. Size remains small.
- Kernel driver cannot be loaded by a standard user: SeLoadDriverPrivilege is admin-only. So user-level distribution is not possible for the driver itself. However: if the org admin preinstalls (e.g., via Intune/GPO), apps run user-level afterwards.
- Also newer: WinFsp 2.1+ supports "ARM64", and there's talk of "FSP as service"? Let me verify details via web search to be accurate, especially size and noinstall/zip availability.

Also worth comparing: appfs requires "Install WinFsp first" (we saw), Cryptomator docs "requires WinFsp, admin rights during installation". Also mention Hvci? Not needed.

Let me search for: "winfsp msi size", "winfsp without admin", "winfsp portable zip noinstall", "projfs enable without admin Client-ProjFS".

# WinFsp

# Frequently Asked Questions

## General

1. *I am running Windows 7 and I am finding that the installed driver is not signed.*

   Your Windows 7 OS is missing SHA-2 Code Signing Support. Make sure it is fully updated.

2. *I cannot run a program located in a WinFsp drive as administrator. I cannot run `regedit.exe` from within a WinFsp drive.*

   When running an executable as administrator, the Windows OS seems to require that the name of the file system that is housing the executable is "NTFS". For example, the MEMFS file system with the command line `memfs-x64.exe -i -F NTFS -m X:` works.

3. *Disconnecting (unmapping) a network drive does not work.*

   You may have Dokany installed. Dokany installs its own Network Provider DLL that unfortunately interferes with the WinFsp handling of network drives. The solution is to change your system’s Network Provider order and ensure that the WinFsp Network Provider runs before the Dokany one. Instructions on how to change the Network Provider order can be found in this [article](https://www.interfacett.com/blogs/changing-the-network-provider-order-in-windows-10/).

4. *Why is the DLL not installed in the Windows system directories?*

   It is true that this would make it convenient to load the DLL, because the Windows loader looks into the Windows system directories when it loads DLL’s. However, in the opinion of the WinFsp author, software that does not ship with the OS should not be installing components in the system directories.

   There are a few alternative methods to overcome this problem. WinFsp recommends marking the WinFsp DLL as "delay load" and then using `FspLoad` to dynamically load the DLL during process initialization. For more information see the WinFsp Tutorial.

5. *Does WinFsp provide debugging symbols?*

   Debugging symbols can be found in the <https://github.com/winfsp/winfsp.sym> repository.

6. *Is there a maximum number of concurrent file systems?*

   WinFsp does not have a hard limit of how many file systems can be created or how many processes can create file systems.

   As of the commits required to fix issue #55, there is however a hash table inside the FSD that uses PID’s (Process ID’s) as keys. This hash table currently expects that in general there will not be more than 50 processes creating file systems. However this is not a hard limit.

## FUSE

1. *Which version of FUSE does WinFsp-FUSE support?*

   It supports both the FUSE 2.8 and FUSE 3.2 API’s. For the FUSE 2.8 API include `<fuse/fuse.h>`. For the FUSE 3.2 API include `<fuse3/fuse.h>`.

2. *FUSE on UNIX systems mounts file systems over an existing directory. When mounting a WinFsp-FUSE file system on a directory, the directory is created and later deleted when the file system goes away. What is the reason for this incompatibility?*

   It would be preferrable if WinFsp-FUSE behaved like FUSE on UNIX in this instance. However there are a number of reasons that this is not the case.

   When mounting over directories in Windows, WinFsp-FUSE uses a special construct called a reparse point. Reparse points are a general mechanism for adding special behavior to files and directories. One of the possible reparse points is the "mountpoint" reparse point (often called "junction"), which converts a directory into a mount point.

   With this in mind here are the reasons for the current WinFsp-FUSE behavior:

   - Symmetry with mounting on a drive. On Windows drives are created when the file system comes into existence and deleted when it is gone.

   - Inability to mount over a non-empty directory on Windows. On FUSE/UNIX this is possible, but not on Windows because NTFS disallows the creation of (mountpoint) reparse points on non-empty directories.

   - Most importantly: inability to guarantee that the mount point will cease to exist if the file system crashes. WinFsp attempts to guarantee that all resources used by a file system will get cleaned up. This is certainly true for the kernel-mode FSD, but an attempt is made to do so also in user mode. For this reason, drive symbolic links are marked as temporary and (importantly for our discussion) mount directories are opened with `FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE`. There is no way to guarantee the removal of a reparse point in the same way.

3. *I have problems getting permissions to work properly in a WinFsp-FUSE file system. Can you help?*

   The WinFsp-FUSE layer includes a built-in command line option that can help: `-o uid=-1`. This instructs the WinFsp-FUSE layer to present all file system files as if they are owned by the user that launched the file system.

   Alternatives include `-o uid=-1,gid=-1`, which presents files as owned by the user **and** group that launched the file system and `-o uid=-1,gid=11`, which presents files as owned by the user that launched the file system and the group "Authenticated Users". (The `fsptool` utility in the `bin` subdirectory of the WinFsp installation directory can be used to convert Windows accounts/SID’s to UID’s and vice versa.)

# WinFsp

# Download

WinFsp is released in the form of an MSI installer that includes a signed driver and all files necessary to run and develop user mode file systems on Windows. The installer supports Windows native, FUSE, .NET and Cygwin file systems out of the box. Download the latest version here.

[Download WinFsp Installer](https://github.com/winfsp/winfsp/releases/download/v2.1/winfsp-2.1.25156.msi)  
[Repository](https://github.com/winfsp/winfsp) · [Changelog](https://github.com/winfsp/winfsp/blob/v2.1/Changelog.md)  

**Additional Downloads**  
WinFsp installation required  

[SSHFS-Win (x64)](https://github.com/winfsp/sshfs-win/releases/download/v3.5.20357/sshfs-win-3.5.20357-x64.msi)  
[SSHFS-Win (x86)](https://github.com/winfsp/sshfs-win/releases/download/v3.5.20357/sshfs-win-3.5.20357-x86.msi)  
[Repository](https://github.com/winfsp/sshfs-win)  

[NFS-Win (x86)](https://github.com/winfsp/nfs-win/releases/download/v1.0.17083/nfs-win-1.0.17083.msi)  
[Repository](https://github.com/winfsp/nfs-win)

## Quick Start Guide

![](install.png)

- Download and run the WinFsp installer.

- In the installer select the option to install the developer files. These include the MEMFS sample file system, but also header and library files that let you develop your own user-mode file system.

- You should not need to reboot, unless WinFsp was already running on your system.

## Launch WinFsp from the Windows Explorer

![](explorer.png)

- Open Windows Explorer

- Select “This PC”. Right-click and select “Map network drive…”

- Map a drive to `\\memfs64\share`. (Assuming a 64-bit machine. Try `\\memfs32\share` if you have a 32-bit machine.)

- After a few seconds a new Explorer window will open up for your new drive.

- The file system behind this drive is a case-insensitive in-memory file system (MEMFS).

- When you are done, you can simply right click on the drive from Windows Explorer and select “Disconnect”.

## Launch WinFsp from the Command Prompt

![](command.png)

- Start a non-admin Command Prompt.

- Navigate to the folder where you installed WinFsp: `cd C:\Program Files (x86)\WinFsp\bin`

- Execute the command: `memfs-x64 -u \memfs64\share2 -m *`. (Assuming a 64-bit machine. Try `memfs-x86 -u \memfs32\share2 -m *` if you have a 32-bit machine.)

- Open a second non-admin Command Prompt and navigate to the new drive.

- When you are done, you can just press Ctrl-C to kill the MEMFS process from the first command prompt.

## For Cygwin users

![](cygwin.png)

The installer includes a FUSE package that can be installed on 32-bit or 64-bit Cygwin. This allows software such as SSHFS and FUSEPY to be built and run on Cygwin with minimal changes.

To install the FUSE package to Cygwin perform the following steps:

```
$ cd opt/cygfuse/       <1>
$ sh ./install.sh       <2>
```

1. From a Cygwin command prompt change to the subdirectory `opt/cygfuse` under the WinFsp installation directory.
2. Execute the command `sh ./install.sh` which will install the necessary FUSE files. This includes FUSE runtime and development files.

To uninstall the FUSE package to Cygwin perform the following steps:

```
$ cd opt/cygfuse/       <1>
$ sh ./uninstall.sh     <2>
```

1. From a Cygwin command prompt change to the subdirectory `opt/cygfuse` under the WinFsp installation directory.
2. Execute the command `sh ./uninstall.sh` which will uninstall all previously installed FUSE files.

# WinFsp

# Commercial License

WinFsp is open source software available under the [GPLv3](https://github.com/winfsp/winfsp/blob/master/License.txt) license with a special exception for Free/Libre and Open Source Software. Entities that wish to use WinFsp without the restrictions imposed by the GPLv3, may alternatively purchase a commercial license.

## License Terms

There are different commercial licenses for organizations and individuals.

### Organizations

The commercial WinFsp license for organizations is as follows:

- It allows a single named team with up to 10 developers to develop with WinFsp.
- It allows unlimited linking and distribution of an organization’s closed-source software products with WinFsp.
- It allows development on multiple closed-source software products.
- It allows use of WinFsp for up to 3 years from the date in the Agreement.
- The license fee is 6000 USD every 3 years. There are no additional royalties.

Alternative license terms for organizations with multiple teams or more than 10 developers are also available.

Please contact Bill Zissimopoulos <billziss at navimatics.com> for more details.

### Individuals

The commercial WinFsp license for individuals is as follows:

- It allows a single named individual to develop with WinFsp. This license cannot be used for a single individual within an organization; an organization license must be purchased instead.
- It allows unlimited linking and distribution of an individual’s closed-source software products with WinFsp.
- It allows development on multiple closed-source software products.
- It allows use of WinFsp for up to 3 years from the date in the Agreement.
- The license fee is 2400 USD every 3 years. There are no additional royalties.

Please contact Bill Zissimopoulos <billziss at navimatics.com> for more details.

## Support

The commercial WinFsp license provides terms for licensing the WinFsp source code and binaries and does not include any support. Public support is available at the following locations:

- [GitHub issues](https://github.com/winfsp/winfsp/issues)
- [WinFsp discussion group](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/winfsp)

Guaranteed priority support under annual contract is also available. Please contact Bill Zissimopoulos <billziss at navimatics.com> for more details.

content.text:
三个问题一次答清(体积 / 用户级分发 / 许可证)：

## 体积：极小

最新版 WinFsp 2025(v2.1,[release 数据](https://api.github.com/repos/winfsp/winfsp/releases/latest)):**MSI 共 2,191,360 字节 ≈ 2.1 MB**,里面打包了签名内核驱动 + 全套开发文件(头文件/库、MEMFS 样例、FUSE/.NET/Cygwin 支持)。对比参考:LayerFS 的 Linux runtime 镜像带 Node 24 + Rust 工具链是 GB 级——WinFsp 本体几乎不构成分发负担。

## 用户级分发：不行，但“管理员装一次，之后全程用户态”

- WinFsp = 内核驱动(`winfsp.sys`)+ launcher 服务，**装驱动必须管理员**(加载驱动需要 SeLoadDriverPrivilege)。没有官方 portable/noinstall 包，release assets 只有 MSI 和一个测试 zip。
- 但**安装之后，运行和挂载完全不需要提权**——官方 Quick Start 就是演示用 *non-admin Command Prompt* 起 MEMFS 挂载。你自己编译的 FS 进程也是普通用户进程。
- 所以业界通行模式(rclone / Cryptomator / SSHFS-Win 都这样)：应用启动时检测 WinFsp 缺失 → 引导用户跑一次 MSI(一次 UAC 弹窗)或企业 Intune/GPO 预装 → 之后一切都是用户态。摩擦点只有“第一次那一次管理员确认”，这也是为什么 LayerFS 们宁可直接 WSL。

## 许可证：GPLv3 + FLOSS 例外，开源可白嫖，闭源链接要交钱

官方 [Commercial License 页](https://winfsp.dev/com/)原文条款：

| 用法 | 代价 |
|---|---|
| 你的项目是**开源**(FLOSS 清单内：MIT/Apache/BSD/MPL 等) | **免费**，FLOSS 例外豁免 GPL 传染 |
| 闭源产品但**不链接**——WinFsp 当独立系统组件，分发原版 MSI 或让用户自装，你的进程与它 arm's-length 交互 | **免费**(mere aggregation,GPL 只管“基于 WinFsp 的作品”) |
| 闭源产品**静态/动态链接** winfsp.dll 或 FUSE API 且随产品分发 | 商业许可：组织 **6000 USD / 3 年**(≤10 名开发者、不限产品、无版税)；个人 **2400 USD / 3 年** |

对比同赛道：

| | 许可 | 闭源嵌入 |
|---|---|---|
| WinFsp | GPLv3 + FLOSS 例外 | 付费或 arm's-length |
| Dokany | **MIT** | 随便用，代价是性能/成熟度略逊 |
| ProjFS | Windows 系统组件，公开 Win32 API | 无许可问题，但前述：写路径拿不到 |

**对 agent-FS 项目的结论**：开源项目(lane、appfs 这类)直接免费用 WinFsp,零成本；闭源商用想内嵌就得算账——6000 USD/3 年在 B2B 产品里不算大，但“引导用户装一次驱动 + GPL 策略”这两件事，正是各家在 Windows 上首选 WSL2 的全部原因。

The user asks: "ProjFS 如何cow" — how would ProjFS do CoW (copy-on-write)? I said earlier ProjFS writes go directly to NTFS and aren't intercepted, so doing CoW requires "thinking of your own solution". The user wants to know: how could you actually implement CoW capture / write isolation with ProjFS?

Let me think about the actual ProjFS API capabilities and known techniques:

ProjFS (Projected File System) API surface:
- `PrjStartVirtualizing` — start a virtualization instance over a root path.
- Directory enumeration callbacks: `PRJ_START_DIRECTORY_ENUMERATION_CB`, `PRJ_GET_DIRECTORY_ENUMERATION_CB`, `PRJ_END_DIRECTORY_ENUMERATION_CB` — provider supplies directory listings on demand.
- `PRJ_GET_PLACEHOLDER_INFO_CB` — provider creates placeholder for a file (metadata only, no content).
- `PRJ_GET_FILE_DATA_CB` — hydration: provider writes file content (`PrjWriteFileData`).
- `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_CB` — notifications! This is the key. You can register for notifications:
  - `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_FILE_OPENED`, `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_FILE_HANDLE_CLOSED_FILE_MODIFIED`, `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_FILE_HANDLE_CLOSED_FILE_DELETED`, `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_FILE_RENAMED`, `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_PRE_DELETE`, `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_PRE_RENAME`, `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_PRE_SET_HARDLINK`, `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_FILE_PRE_CONVERT_TO_FULL`, etc.
  - Crucially there's `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_FILE_PRE_CONVERT_TO_FULL` — fired when a placeholder is about to be converted to a full file (i.e., a write to a hydrated placeholder is about to happen). The provider can **fail** this notification (return HRESULT error), which **blocks the conversion** — this is the "write blocking" hook!
  - `PRJ_NOTIFY_TYPES` also include `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_PRECONVERT_ON_HANDLE_OPEN?` Hmm. The main ones: UseNegativePathCache, notification mask per file via PrjFillPlaceholderInfo notifications param.

Known technique for CoW with ProjFS (this is exactly what VFS for Git did for its "modified files" tracking, and what people building "dehydrate/revert" do):

1. **Fail PRE_CONVERT_TO_FULL to block in-place writes**, forcing the writer to... hmm, actually if you fail it, the write fails (ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED-ish) — that gives you write *protection* (read-only projection), not CoW.

2. **Copy-up dance (the actual CoW recipe)**:
   - On `PRJ_NOTIFICATION_FILE_PRE_CONVERT_TO_FULL` (write about to land on a placeholder): you can't redirect the write to another path in the same handle operation. The write goes to that path.
   - So real CoW with ProjFS must be done differently: you let writes land on NTFS, but you **capture the original bytes before** (you have them in your provider store — you're the one who hydrated!) and treat the NTFS write as the "upper layer". 
   - I.e., ProjFS's natural architecture: **lower layer = your provider's data store** (on-demand projected); **upper layer = the real NTFS files once modified/created**. The overlay IS the working directory. Directory enumeration = union of provider namespace + on-disk full files (ProjFS automatically shows full files; placeholders get superseded when converted to full). Deleted files can be handled via notifications recording tombstones, and hidden with... hmm, you can project over them? If a file is deleted, the notification `FILE_HANDLE_CLOSED_FILE_DELETED` tells you; you can then project the placeholder again (reproject) or record the deletion.
   - To "commit or discard": discard = delete the modified full files and re-project placeholders (dehydrate via `PrjDeleteFile` + recreate placeholder, or `PrjWritePlaceholderInfo` again); commit = copy the modified files back to your store.
   - This is exactly "working tree as overlay, store as base" — merge with what I said: "写落到 NTFS 真实文件——是虚拟工作树不是 overlay" — actually it IS usable as an overlay where the NTFS dir is the upper layer and the provider is the lower layer! The subtlety: writes aren't *intercepted and redirected*, they land in place; you detect them via notifications and diff via... how do you know the final bytes? At handle-close-modified time you can read the file. Or use `PrjGetOnDiskFileState`.

3. Multi-agent parallel lanes with ProjFS: one virtualization instance per lane directory, all backed by the same provider store. Each lane = its own NTFS directory where modified files materialize. Instant "fork" = just create a new empty lane directory and start virtualizing the same base view. No copying — exactly the LayerFS-style benefit. Diff = compare materialized full files + tombstones vs base.

4. Limitations of this approach:
   - **Renamed/deleted/new files**: notifications cover it (FILE_RENAMED, FILE_HANDLE_CLOSED_FILE_DELETED, new files just exist as full files — enumeration must merge provider entries + on-disk entries; ProjFS handles full files in the root natively? For files not in your projection: they show up as normal files; the provider's GetDirectoryEnumeration callback gets asked for provider items; on-disk items also appear. There's a subtlety: items that exist both places — full file wins (that's the overlay semantics).
   - **Partial writes / in-place modification of hydrated file**: the file converts to full; you diff at commit time.
   - **Hard to get byte-level ops**: you get file-level semantics (open/close/modify notifications), not every write. For agent review that's arguably better (file-level diff).
   - **Cannot redirect writes elsewhere** (no upper-dir-in-another-location): the working dir itself accumulates the changes. So "review then apply" = diff working dir against store, then either keep (commit) or revert (delete + reproject placeholders = instant, no copy).
   - Case sensitivity, ACL: NTFS.
   - Only works where the tree is projected by you (the base must be your store, not an arbitrary existing folder). To overlay an **existing** host folder (AgentFS-style `agentfs run claude` over an existing repo), ProjFS can't intercept reads of existing NTFS files — placeholders only. You'd have to build your store from the repo first (import), then project into an empty dir. That's the LayerFS Init flow actually (import → project).
   - Negative path cache, PrjGetVirtualizationInstanceInfo, etc. details.

Also worth mentioning: this is literally how VFS for Git tracked modifications (it used ProjFS notifications to know which files changed so `git status` could be fast — "modified paths" via notifications). And Microsoft's docs page "Handling View Changes" covers how the provider learns about modifications (notifications) — I found that link in an earlier search result ("Handling View Changes - learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/projfs/handling-view-changes").

So the answer: ProjFS 的 CoW = "投影即 lower,工作目录即 upper":
- 读路径:on-demand hydration(这已经是 CoW 的"读不算复制")。
- 写路径:不拦截、不重定向,写把 placeholder **convert to full**(NTFS 原生速度);PRE_CONVERT_TO_FULL 通知给你最后一个否决点(可以做只读保护)。
- 变更感知:notification 回调(opened / handle-closed-modified / deleted / renamed / pre-*)→ 记 tombstone、标记 dirty。
- 提交:close-modified 时读回文件内容入库(diff vs base 只传变更块,看你 store)。
- 丢弃:删掉 full file + 重新投影 placeholder(`PrjDeleteFile`/重新 `PrjWritePlaceholderInfo`)→ 瞬间回滚,零拷贝。
- 多 lane:同一 store,多个虚拟化实例 = 多个并行 agent 工作区,fork = 空目录 + start virtualizing。
- 对比 overlayfs 语义缺什么:写不能重定向到别处(工作目录自己变脏,想保持 base 干净必须"store 为 base、空目录投影"模式);只有文件级通知没有块级;PrjNotification 不能给你写入内容本身;删除/重命名要靠 tombstone 自绘;未投影的既有文件无法被捕获(必须先导入)。以及 Windows-only,1809+,需一次性启用 Client-ProjFS 功能(管理员一次)。

   - I.e., ProjFS's natural architecture: **lower layer = your provider's data store** (on-demand projected); **upper layer = the real NTFS files once modified/created**. The overlay IS the working directory. Directory enumeration = union of provider namespace + on-disk full files (ProjFS automatically shows full files; placeholders get superseded when converted to full). Deleted files can be handled via notifications recording tombstones, and hidden with... hmm, you can project over them? If a file is deleted, the notification `FILE_HANDLE_CLOSED_FILE_DELETED` tells you; you can then project the placeholder again (reproject) or record the deletion.

The subtlety: writes aren't *intercepted and redirected*, they land in place; you detect them via notifications and diff via... how do you know the final bytes? At handle-close-modified time you can read the file. Or use `PrjGetOnDiskFileState`.

Diff = compare materialized full files + tombstones vs base.

- 提交:close-modified 时读回文件内容入库(diff vs base 只传变更块,看你 store)。

Core reframing: ProjFS 不能"拦截并重定向写",所以 CoW 的做法不是 overlayfs 式的"写时复制到别处",而是把架构倒过来:**你的 store 是 lower(按需投影),工作目录自己长成 upper(写就地物化成 full 文件),CoW 的"W"发生在读路径(hydration)和回滚路径(re-project)**。

Recipe:

1. **读 CoW(免费获得)**:文件以 placeholder(元数据,1KB 级)存在,读才回调 GET_FILE_DATA 写内容。base 不占盘、fork 不拷贝。

2. **写 = 物化,不拦截**:
   - 写 placeholder → Windows 自动 "convert to full"(NTFS 原生速度);
   - 提供方收通知:FILE_PRE_CONVERT_TO_FULL(可以否决 = 只读保护)、HANDLE_CLOSED_FILE_MODIFIED / DELETED / RENAMED、PRE_DELETE / PRE_RENAME;
   - 新建文件 = 普通 NTFS 文件,枚举时与投影条目合并,full 文件覆盖 placeholder —— 这天然就是 overlay 的 "upper 覆盖 lower" 语义。

3. **变更台账**:通知回调记 tombstone(删除)、dirty 集(修改)、新增集合(枚举 diff 或扫描 on-disk full files)。这就是 VFS for Git 的 modified-paths 机制(它当年就用 ProjFS 通知让 git status 秒回)。

4. **commit**:HANDLE_CLOSED_FILE_MODIFIED 时读回文件 → 存 store(ContentID = 内容 hash,docs 原文就是这么举例的)。

5. **discard / 回滚**:PrjDeleteFile(带 PRJ_UPDATE_ALLOW_DIRTY_DATA)删掉脏文件 → 枚举重新投影旧版 placeholder;瞬间、零拷贝 —— 这就是 discard overlay 的等价物。tombstone 同理(删除记录清除 = 重新投影)。

6. **多 agent 并行 lane**:ContentID 版本信息 + 每个视图一个虚拟化实例,同一 backing store,docs 原文的 timestamp-view 例子就是 branch 语义(视图=commit 时间点)。fork = 空目录 + PrjMarkDirectoryAsPlaceholder + start virtualizing。这就是 LayerFS 的 Workspace/branch 结构,只不过 upper 不是单独目录而是工作目录本身。

7. **缺什么(和 overlayfs/WinFsp 比)**:
   - 工作目录会真实落盘变脏 —— 想保护"宿主原有目录"做不到:ProjFS 只能投影你 store 里的东西,不能把一个既有 NTFS 目录变成受监控 overlay(base 必须先导入 store)。LayerFS/AgentFS 的"盖在宿主目录上"模式做不了。

A mermaid diagram might help show the architecture. Flow: agent writes → placeholder converts to full → notification → ledger; commit reads back to store; discard = PrjDeleteFile + reproject. Could do a compact mermaid flowchart. Yes, include one small mermaid.

Keep terse. Cite: MS docs handling-view-changes, projected-file-system overview.

元数据 ~KB 级] --"读:GET_FILE_DATA 回调"--> H[hydrated] H --"写:自动 convert to full
NTFS 原生速度"--> F[full 脏文件] end S[(backing store
ContentID = 内容 hash)] --"投影"--> P N["通知回调
PRE_CONVERT_TO_FULL / CLOSED_MODIFIED
/ DELETED / RENAMED"] --> L[(变更台账
dirty / tombstone / new)] F --"commit:读回入库"--> S F --"discard:PrjDeleteFile
ALLOW_DIRTY_DATA"--> P L --> S ``` 1. **读路径的 CoW 是白送的**：文件以 placeholder 存在(只占元数据)，首次读才回调 `PRJ_GET_FILE_DATA` 给内容。base 不落盘、fork 零拷贝。 2. **写路径不拦截，只记账**：写 placeholder 会自动物化成 full 文件;`PRJ_NOTIFICATION_CB` 给你 `FILE_PRE_CONVERT_TO_FULL`(可返回错误否决 = 免费的只读保护)、`HANDLE_CLOSED_FILE_MODIFIED/DELETED/REANAMED`。新建文件就是普通 NTFS 文件，枚举时与投影条目自动合并、full 覆盖 placeholder——**这正是 overlay 的“upper 盖 lower”语义**。记成 dirty / tombstone / new 三本台账。(VFS for Git 当年就用这套通知做 modified-paths,让 `git status` 在 300GB 仓库上秒回。) 3. **commit** = 台账驱动:CLOSED_MODIFIED 时把文件读回 store,`ContentID` 存内容 hash(文档原示例)。 4. **discard / 回滚** = `PrjDeleteFile`(带 `PRJ_UPDATE_ALLOW_DIRTY_DATA`)删掉脏文件，下次枚举重新投影旧 placeholder——**瞬间、零拷贝**，等价于扔掉 overlay 的 upper 目录。tombstone 清除即文件复活。 5. **多 agent 并行 lane** = 同一 store,每个 lane 一个空目录 + `PrjMarkDirectoryAsPlaceholder` + 各自视图。文档的 `PRJ_PLACEHOLDER_VERSION_INFO`(128 字节 ContentID + 时间戳视图切换 `PrjUpdateFileIfNeeded`)本质上就是 **branch/checkout 原语**:`ContentID` 没变就不动盘上文件。 ## 结构性缺口(相对 WinFsp/overlayfs) - **盖不住宿主既有目录**：ProjFS 只能投影你自己 store 里的东西，不能把一个已存在的 NTFS 目录变成受监控 overlay——想要 LayerFS/AgentFS 那种“`agentfs run` 直接罩住你的 repo”,必须先把 repo 导入 store 再投影到新目录(LayerFS 的 Init 流程恰好就是这个形状)。 - **事件粒度是文件级**，拿不到写入字节流；commit 要自己读回文件。 - **脏数据真实占盘**：upper 就是工作目录本身，无内容级去重——LayerFS 那种 166× 去重只能靠 store 侧自己chunk。 - 通知覆盖有边角(部分水合 + mmap 写的 conversion 路径要小心测)，Windows 10 1809+,管理员一次性启用 `Client-ProjFS` 功能。 结论:ProjFS 能做 CoW,只是 CoW 的语义从“写时复制”变成“**读时物化 + 写时记账 + 弃时重投影**”。对“每 agent 一条 lane、commit/discard、秒级 fork”这个场景够用且性能模型更好(热路径全是原生 NTFS);缺的是“零导入罩住现有目录”和写路径拦截，而那两样恰恰是 WinFsp 的强项——两者其实是互补而非竞争。

| 项 | git 是否共享 | 占用 |

| | 模型 | 冷文件 | 读密集(build/grep 全树) | 每 agent 磁盘 |
|---|---|---|---|---|

content.thinking:
The user asks: "可以 实时winfsp 系列 然后再 layerfs 中适配吗" — a bit garbled. Interpretation: "可以试试 WinFsp 系列,然后再在 LayerFS 中适配吗?" — Can we try the WinFsp series (lane/AgentFS), and then adapt it into LayerFS? Or: "Can WinFsp be adapted into LayerFS?" — i.e., use WinFsp as a mount backend for LayerFS so it runs natively on Windows instead of WSL.

So the question: feasibility of adapting LayerFS to WinFsp (native Windows Store execution via WinFsp), possibly after trying the WinFsp-based tools (lane/AgentFS).

This is a technical feasibility analysis. Let me think hard about what LayerFS actually is architecturally and what a WinFsp port would require:

From research:
- LayerFS core: Rust (`core/` workspace, `layerfs-daemon` binary, `layerfs-node` native addon (N-API for the JS SDK)). The daemon implements FUSE (libfuse) — workspace mounts inside Sandbox containers (Docker, Linux). The Store is SQLite. Content-addressed objects. Workspaces are FUSE mounts in the daemon's process inside sandbox containers.
- Architecture: agent bash calls → `layerfs` CLI → JS SDK (`@layerfs/agent`) → native addon (`layerfs.node`, N-API) → Store (SQLite) + workspace mount via daemon.
- Sandboxes = Docker containers with FUSE. `workspace.mount` → daemon in container mounts FUSE view; exec runs command in the mount; commit; unmount.
- File tools (read/write/edit/grep) go through SDK in-process, NOT through the FS.

So porting to Windows with WinFsp requires:

1. **The Store**: SQLite — cross-platform, fine on Windows. But it stores POSIX metadata (mode bits, uid/gid, symlinks, hardlinks). Windows port needs a POSIX-metadata-in-database approach (metadata lives in Store, not in NTFS) — actually fine since Store is SQLite. The issue is the FUSE view: they need to present POSIX semantics via WinFsp (WinFsp supports POSIX-ish semantics; FUSE layer supports uid/gid mapping — the FAQ we read mentions `-o uid=-1` etc.).

2. **The mount layer**: replace libfuse with WinFsp. Options:
   a. WinFsp's **FUSE compatibility layer** (it supports FUSE 2.8 and FUSE 3.2 APIs per the FAQ we read!). LayerFS's daemon is Rust — uses libfuse (fuse backend? Actually it might use the `fuser` crate or libfuse3 C bindings). The FAQ mentions Cygwin FUSE package — so WinFsp-FUSE works with POSIX FUSE programs **under Cygwin**. For a native Rust daemon, there's the question: does WinFsp's FUSE layer work for native Windows FUSE apps? WinFsp provides `fuse3/fuse.h` headers and a DLL for native (non-Cygwin) use too — yes, WinFsp-FUSE has a native (MSVC/MinGW) personality. There are Rust crates: `winfsp` crate? There's a Rust binding to WinFsp (e.g., `winfsp` crate by Russ) — and the `fuser` crate is Linux/macOS (fuser uses /dev/fuse on Linux; on Windows fuser added WinFsp backend! fuser 0.15 has WinFsp support? Actually fuser 0.15 added WinFsp backend via the winfsp crate — yes I recall fuser merged optional WinFsp support. Let me verify with a search — fuser 0.15 "Add WinFsp backend" PR #211? I believe fuser ≥0.15 supports Windows via WinFsp (with limitations). If LayerFS uses fuser crate, the port might be surprisingly feasible. But LayerFS builds only for Linux targets (musl? their .cargo/config.toml ARM64 profile). Their pjdfstest conformance — they'd need to drop some POSIX semantics on Windows.

3. **The Sandbox problem**: LayerFS's execution model = commands run inside Docker Sandboxes where the FUSE mount lives. On native Windows, Docker containers are Linux VMs again — but wait: if Store runs natively on Windows, the Sandbox container needs access to the mount. Two options:
   - Sandboxes stay Linux containers with their own FUSE daemon + Store access via... the Store is SQLite on Windows FS — SQLite over network/volume into container is fragile (they explicitly prohibit /mnt/c and Docker-Desktop-volume topologies for locking reasons).
   - Or restructure: mounts on the Windows host via WinFsp, commands run natively (no sandbox) — that's a major model change (LayerFS couples mount+exec+commit inside sandbox).
   
   This is the deep coupling: in LayerFS, `workspace.mount` mounts in the sandbox's daemon; exec runs there. Windows-native would need either (a) sandbox containers accessing a Windows-hosted store (network FS into container / VirtioFS share — 9p/virtiofs, perf + locking issues), or (b) dropping sandbox-virtualization, mounting via WinFsp on host, running commands on host — that's basically lane/AgentFS's simpler model, losing "ephemeral computing in containers".

4. **The fork/exec, /proc, hardlink etc. Rust code**: daemon code is presumably full of Unix-isms (unshare? no — sandboxes are containers; daemon in container uses fork/exec, signals). Porting layerfs-daemon to compile for MSVC/mingw: nontrivial but bounded.

5. **Effort estimate**: The pragmatic path is NOT "port LayerFS to WinFsp" but "give LayerFS a Windows adapter at the SDK/daemon boundary" — actually they already did that: the Windows adapter runs the whole Linux stack in a WSL worker. A WinFsp-native port = new daemon target + sandbox story redesign + POSIX conformance relaxation + CI matrix. For an unpaid lab project, they chose WSL. For the user: adapting LayerFS to WinFsp themselves = forking LayerFS core (Rust, sizeable codebase) — big but doable; the more economical path is:
   - Use lane/AgentFS now (WinFsp-native, solves the space problem),
   - If they want LayerFS semantics (branches, publish, multi-machine store), LayerFS already runs on Windows via WSL2 — "适配" already exists (the worker adapter).

So answer structure:
1. 直接回答:技术上可行(WinFsp 有 FUSE 兼容层,fuser 有 WinFsp 后端),但"把 LayerFS 适配到 WinFsp"不是换挂载后端一件事,而是三件事:挂载层替换、Sandbox 执行模型重构、POSIX 语义降级。
2. 可行性拆解表:每层要动什么、难度。
3. 两条现实路径:A. 混合(推荐):LayerFS Store/分支语义留在 WSL(官方已支持)或直接用 lane/AgentFS 干活;B. 真原生:fork LayerFS core 做 WinFsp daemon —— 工作量估计、最大坑(沙箱耦合、SQLite 锁在跨 VM 边界、pjdfstest 语义)。
4. 建议顺序:先试 lane/AgentFS(零改动,立刻解决 worktree 空间),要 branch/merge/publish 再上 LayerFS(WSL 适配已存在),真要原生 WinFsp 版 LayerFS 就是个 fork 项目。

URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ephemeral-AI-Lab/layerfs/main/core/Cargo.toml
Content-Type: text/plain
Method: text

# Independent replacement-product workspace (LayerFS v1.1.0).
#
# The reference workspace at the repository root keeps its own members, lockfile
# and target directory; `core/` is excluded there. The candidate components under
# implementation are layerfs-telemetry (timer), layerfs-content (C1) and
# layerfs-storage (C2). Further packages are added with their real boundaries.
# Third-party pins are added with the component that needs them.

[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = [
    "crates/layerfs-content",
    "crates/layerfs-storage",
    "crates/layerfs-persistence",
    "crates/layerfs-project",
    "crates/layerfs-history",
    "crates/layerfs-telemetry",
    "crates/layerfs-overlay",
    "crates/layerfs-workspace",
    "crates/layerfs-store-service",
    "crates/layerfs-daemon",
    "crates/layerfs-api",
    "crates/layerfs-bridge",
    "crates/layerfs-sandbox",
    "crates/layerfs-fuse",
    # Node binding of the JavaScript SDK (owner-approved napi-rs, 2026-10-15).
    "../api/binding",
]
exclude = [
    "vendor/fuser-0.18.0",
]

[workspace.package]
edition = "2021"
version = "1.1.0"
rust-version = "1.85"
license = "MIT"

# Keep the large boundary fixtures cheap without removing cases or assertions.
# Product dev/release profiles and test debug assertions stay unchanged.
[profile.test]
opt-level = 1

[profile.test.package.zstd-sys]
opt-level = 3

# Owner-authorized signed-timestamp correction to the crates.io 0.18.0 archive.
[patch.crates-io]
fuser = { version = "=0.18.0", path = "vendor/fuser-0.18.0" }
